name: Five-Allergen-free Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of home cooking made without peanuts and tree nuts, eggs, dairy, shellfish and sesame, from Mexican pipián and pozole to Canadian salmon, a Greek chicken and bean stew and a Japanese-style tofu curry. It does use wheat, soy, fish and mustard, with seeds, fortified soy drink, tofu and lean meat doing the jobs of nuts, eggs and dairy.
howItWorks:
**Five left out, on purpose.** Made without peanuts and tree nuts, eggs, dairy, shellfish and sesame. It does use wheat, soy, fish and mustard, plus flax and sunflower and pumpkin seeds, so it does not suit anyone who avoids those. Some people with a nut or sesame allergy react to other seeds too, so ask your allergist first. **This plan does not replace your allergist's advice.**

**Calcium, choline, vitamin D and B12.** Soy drink, calcium-set tofu, canned fish with soft bones and greens share calcium. Choline is hard, so chicken, beef, fish, tofu and edamame turn up in most meals. Salmon, sardines and soy drink carry vitamin D and B12, but vitamin D and iodine stay low, so the salt is iodized; ask about a supplement. It does not suit a kidney diet.

**Read every label.** Check the ingredient list and any "may contain" line each time you buy, since a missing warning does not guarantee safety. Hidden milk, egg, nuts or sesame turn up in bread, pasta, broth, spice blends, ground spices, dried chiles, seed butters, soy yogurt, oats and flax. Buy them packaged, never from bulk bins or bakery counters, and ask the maker if an allergy is severe.

**Keep it clean at home.** If anyone in the house eats nuts, sesame, egg or dairy, cook these recipes first. Wash hands with soap and water (sanitiser gel does not remove allergens), and wash boards, knives, pans and counters. Use a fresh spoon in the seed butter jar and the soy yogurt tub, and a separate toaster or toaster bags.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Pipián, Greek stew, beef soup and pozole each make two portions. At Light the second snack drops and grains, bread, potato and oil shrink while meat, fish and tofu stay about the same, so rice and rye are only a spoonful or half a slice; skip them if you like. Big adds a snack a day. Fibre runs high, so build up slowly and drink water.

name: Bean Kitchen (Light)
summary: Beans and lentils at most meals, done well: a three-bean chili, a hummus plate, a lentil and squash dal, Tuscan white beans, a black bean stew and two fish dinners. No bread, rice or pasta, just beans, potatoes, sweet potato, squash and oats.
howItWorks:
**Beans at most meals.** Chili, dal, Tuscan beans, black bean stew and a chicken and chickpea stew each make two portions. A hummus plate, a white bean and tuna salad, a sweet potato and pinto bean bowl and a lentil dinner fill the gaps.

**Easing into beans.** This plan is high in fibre on purpose. If beans are new to you, start with smaller portions, drink water through the day and give your gut a week or two to settle. Rinse canned beans well. The dal and the edamame are the gentlest places to begin. With a sensitive gut or a health condition, check with a dietitian first.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's chili, Wednesday's dal, Thursday's Tuscan beans, Friday's black bean stew and Saturday's chicken stew each become the next day's lunch. **Sunday prep:** blend the hummus and boil Monday's egg, and Monday's lunch is a five-minute job.

**Fish, eggs and sardines.** Ginger-soy salmon on Tuesday and lemon trout on Sunday bring omega-3 and some **vitamin D**, which is hard to get from food alone. A firm egg on Monday's and Wednesday's lunch and Thursday's baked egg carry your **choline**, and sardines on Thursday and Friday add protein, niacin and calcium. These days run bean-heavy, and they close the gaps.

**Sizes.** Light drops the second snack and trims the oats, beef, chicken and potatoes; the fish, eggs and sardines stay. Big adds a snack and bigger portions, so on the bean-heaviest days fibre runs to more than double the usual daily target. Build up slowly.

name: Big Bowls (Light)
summary: Every main meal is a bowl: a base of quinoa, lentils, sweet potato or an intact grain, a protein, lots of vegetables and a sauce worth eating. Salmon, trout and canned salmon bring the omega-3, and four of the bowls make enough for tomorrow's lunch.
howItWorks:
**Base, protein, veg, sauce.** Every lunch and dinner follows the same build: a whole-food base (quinoa, barley, buckwheat, beans, lentils or sweet potato), a protein, a pile of vegetables and a sauce that ties it together. No bread, rice or pasta, so the fibre stays high.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's black bean bowl, Wednesday's lentil and beet bowl, Thursday's shawarma bowl and Saturday's beef bowl each make two portions for the next day's lunch. Reheat only the grain and the hot protein, and add egg, slaw, crema and avocado cold.

**Fish four times.** Teriyaki-style salmon on Tuesday, lemon-herb trout on Friday, and canned salmon in Saturday's bowl and Sunday's spiced cakes bring the omega-3 and some vitamin D. Legumes, eggs, chicken, tuna and beef cover the protein, and almonds, walnuts or seeds land every day for vitamin E. Eggs show up where the day needs choline: the black bean bowl, the beet bowl, the hash and two snack plates.

**Two short preps.** Mix each oats jar the night before, or Wednesday's and Friday's together on Tuesday night. Cook a little extra quinoa with Friday's trout for Saturday's lunch. Cooked grains cool within 1 hour and keep up to 3 days.

**What changes with size.** Light keeps the same bowls with the same chicken, beef, canned fish, eggs, yogurt and most of the beans and lentils. What shrinks is the grain, the oil and the nuts, and most snacks drop. Tuesday's salmon and Friday's trout are about half a regular fillet across Light.

**Grain and Big.** Near 1,600 kcal the grain under each bowl is about half a Standard portion; at 1,400 it is a couple of spoonfuls on most days, and the beans, vegetables and spinach fill the bowl. Big grows the bases and adds a snack on three days."

name: Budget Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of beans, lentils, eggs, canned fish, chicken thighs, frozen vegetables and oats, cooked the way Mexico, India, Italy and Canada do it: smoky pinto chili, red lentil dal, sardine pasta and salmon patties. Big pots and planned leftovers keep the shopping list short, and nothing goes to waste.
howItWorks:
**One pot, then leftovers.** Monday's pinto bean chili makes three portions: dinner Monday, lunch Tuesday and a frozen portion for Sunday night. Every other dinner makes two, so each cook feeds two meals. Sunday prep: soak the pinto beans, and cook and chill the brown rice for Monday's fried rice.

**Canned fish and pantry protein.** Canned salmon with its soft bones on Wednesday and sardines on Friday bring omega-3, calcium and vitamin D, and each becomes the next day's lunch. Beans, lentils, eggs and chicken thighs carry the rest of the protein and iron.

**Frozen veg, nothing wasted.** Frozen peas, corn, spinach, broccoli and berries keep for months and cover vitamin C, vitamin K and folate. Cabbage, carrots, potatoes, onions, bananas and yogurt each turn up in several dishes, so nothing is left to wilt in the fridge.

**Every nutrient still lands.** Milk and yogurt carry the calcium alongside the canned fish. Spinach, lentils and beans bring iron, peanut butter and canola oil bring vitamin E, canola and canned fish bring omega-3, and eggs, chicken and milk bring choline. Oats, beans and whole grains keep the fibre high and the glycaemic load steady.

**What changes with size.** Light trims the oats, rice, lentils, oil and chicken, and keeps one snack on six days (none on Wednesday). Big grows those portions and adds a snack on four days. Big is rich in calcium already, so ask your care provider before adding a calcium supplement on top.

name: Budget Vegetarian (Light)
summary: A week of meatless pots built on beans, lentils, eggs and yogurt: Italian minestrone, red lentil dal, a cabbage and chickpea curry, shakshuka, a potato frittata and black bean tacos. One big pot or pan often feeds two meals, and nothing goes to waste.
howItWorks:
**One pot, then leftovers.** Monday's minestrone makes three portions: dinner, Tuesday's lunch and one for the freezer, moved to the fridge on Saturday night. The curry, shakshuka sauce, dal, frittata and tacos each make two, so every lunch from Tuesday on is cooked. Soak the black beans on Friday night.

**Staples keep the list short.** Beans, lentils, oats, brown rice, potatoes, eggs and yogurt carry the week, with frozen peas, spinach and berries. Cabbage, onions and carrots turn up in several dishes so nothing wilts, and cheese is only a garnish. New to this many beans? Drink plenty of water.

**B12 from eggs and dairy.** Plants don't make **B12**, so every day has an egg dish and yogurt or milk, which also bring choline. Vitamin D is hard to get from food, more so without fish. Health Canada advises a daily 400 IU supplement after 50; at any age, ask your care provider.

**Iron, zinc and omega-3 from plants.** These are absorbed or converted less well from plants than from meat or fish, so beans, lentils, eggs and seeds turn up every day, with lime, tomato or pepper beside the iron. Flax, walnuts and canola bring ALA, which the body turns into fish-type omega-3 only in small amounts.

**What changes with size.** Light drops the second snack and trims the rice, oats, tortillas, oil and cheese. Big grows every portion, and its milk and yogurt already carry plenty of calcium, so check with your care provider before adding a calcium supplement on top.

name: Caribbean Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Caribbean home cooking: ackee and saltfish, jerk chicken with rice and peas, curry channa, run down mackerel, Cuban black bean soup with chicken, Haitian lime-marinated chicken and a Saturday curry goat. Brown rice, plantain and yuca for the carbs, Scotch bonnet, thyme and allspice for the soul, and plenty of lime.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's jerk chicken, Tuesday's curry channa, Wednesday's run down mackerel, Thursday's black bean soup, Friday's lime-marinated chicken and Saturday's curry goat each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. The shrimp, snapper and breakfasts are cooked fresh.

**Fatty fish three times.** Run down mackerel on Wednesday (it comes back at Thursday's lunch) and sardines on toast on Sunday carry your **omega-3 and B12**, and they help with **vitamin D**. Ackee and saltfish, shrimp and snapper round out the seafood.

**The Sunday before.** Soak the week's dry kidney beans and black beans in separate bowls on Saturday night (the Prep screen gives the amounts for your size). On Sunday, simmer each with a bay leaf until tender, about 1 hour. Leave them unsalted, since each dish brings its own salt. They keep 4 to 5 days chilled, so freeze a tub. Cook brown rice fresh, about 40 minutes.

**Whole-food carbs, Caribbean style.** Brown rice, whole-wheat flatbread and dumplings, yuca and plantain do the work, with beans or chickpeas most days. Plantain is boiled or baked, never fried, and coconut milk is a spoonful at a time. The warm milk with the eggs, banana milk and peanut punch carry **calcium**.

**Pickles and heat.** Pikliz, escovitch pickle, lime and Scotch bonnet brighten the rich dishes. Make the pikliz on Thursday night, and start the salt cod soaking a day ahead, on Sunday, Wednesday and Saturday.

name: Chicken Every Way (Light)
summary: Five chicken dinners that taste nothing alike: a Moroccan-style tagine, a Greek lemon-oregano grill, a barley soup, a sweet potato curry and a Sunday-style roast. Salmon and trout bring the omega-3, and the carbs are all whole foods.
howItWorks:
**Chicken, five ways.** Thighs go into Monday's tagine-style stew, breast into Tuesday's Greek grill and Friday's curry, drumsticks into Wednesday's barley soup and mixed legs into Saturday's roast. Each dish has its own spices and method, so no two taste alike.

**Cook once, eat twice.** The stew, soup, curry and roast each make two portions, and the second is the next day's lunch. Cool it within the hour, keep it up to 3 days and reheat it to 74 °C. Salmon and trout are always cooked fresh.

**Fish three times.** Sardines on Monday, salmon on Thursday and trout on Sunday bring **omega-3** and a little **vitamin D**. Wednesday's tuna lunch is a lighter extra. Eggs appear at three breakfasts and two lunches, and the carbs stay whole: oats, quinoa, barley, potatoes, beans and fruit.

**Light.** It covers 1400 to 1800 kcal. It keeps one snack a day and trims the oats, barley, oil, nuts and potatoes first, while kale and spinach stay for calcium and iron. The fish and most chicken hold; at 1400 the Greek chicken breast is about half size and the roast legs a third smaller.

**Big.** It grows the chicken, fish, eggs, beans, grains, dairy, oil and nuts, and adds an orange and banana snack on Monday and apricots with almonds on Thursday. The vegetables and fruit in the dishes stay about the same.

name: Chinese Home Cooking (Light)
summary: A week at the Chinese home table: congee and egg pancakes for breakfast, mapo tofu, red-braised beef, steamed fish and homemade dumplings for dinner, with mixed brown rice, whole-wheat noodles and plenty of greens.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's mapo tofu, Wednesday's chicken stir-fry, Friday's red-braised beef and Saturday's dumplings each make two portions, so Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday and Sunday lunches are done. The millet porridge also feeds two breakfasts.

**Rice twice.** On Sunday, simmer 2 cups of brown rice with 1 cup of pearled barley and 6 cups of water for 45 minutes, then rest it for 10. On Thursday, cook half that. Extra freezes well. Roast the snack sweet potatoes on Sunday, too.

**Fish three times.** Scallion oil salmon on Tuesday and doubanjiang mackerel on Thursday carry the **omega-3 and vitamin D**, never on back-to-back days. Steamed sea bass on Sunday adds lean protein. Walnuts blended into soy milk, on the millet porridge and with pear help the balance, too.

**Tofu, greens and soy milk.** Calcium-set tofu, soy milk, gai lan, bok choy and napa do the calcium work without dairy. Eggs, shrimp and iodized salt help with iodine, and almonds and peanuts cover vitamin E.

**Salt with care.** Soy sauce, oyster sauce and doubanjiang are strong, so each recipe measures them, and black vinegar, ginger, scallion and Sichuan pepper's numbing tingle add the punch instead. Saturday is the long day, with the dumplings, and Friday's beef is hands-off but long.

name: Comfort Classics, Lighter (Light)
summary: The food people crave, built to the framework: shepherd's pie, fish pie, chicken pot pie under a potato crust, meatballs with gravy, meatloaf and a white chicken chili with all the toppings. Sauces are thickened with beans, cauliflower and potato, not flour, and cheddar is only a garnish.
howItWorks:
**Comfort, rebuilt.** Shepherd's pie, fish pie, chicken pot pie, meatballs and gravy, meatloaf and a white chicken chili are all here, with no flour. Potato crusts and mashes, and sauces thickened with blended beans, cauliflower and potato, do the work. Cheddar is a small garnish, never a layer.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's shepherd's pie, Wednesday's chili, Thursday's meatballs and Saturday's pot pie each make two portions, so Tuesday, Thursday, Friday and Sunday lunches are done. Weeknight dinners take about 40 minutes. Saturday's pot pie is the one weekend project.

**Fish and protein.** Salmon in Tuesday's fish pie and Friday's roast fillet carries your omega-3 and some **vitamin D**, always cooked fresh. Beef, chicken, turkey, salmon, beans and lentils carry the lunches and dinners, and milk, nuts and seeds the oatmeal breakfasts. Eggs sit in three breakfasts, and the fish pie, meatballs and meatloaf use some.

**Light.** It covers 1400 to 1800 kcal and drops one snack a day. At 1400 the oats, nuts, oil, cheddar, potatoes and beans get smaller, so the pies keep a real topping but the mash is mostly cauliflower. The turkey trims by up to a third, the chicken and salmon by less. The beef, eggs and other vegetables stay about as written.

**Big.** It keeps every snack and adds a guacamole snack on Monday and Thursday. The meat, fish, dairy, beans, lentils and nuts grow by about half to three quarters, and the potatoes, sweet potatoes, oats and oil by up to about double; the scramble gets a third or fourth egg. The other vegetables, squash and fruit stay the same. Use a wider pot for the two-portion dishes.

name: Dairy-free East Asian (Light)
summary: A week of Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese home cooking that is naturally dairy-free, with calcium from greens, small fish eaten with their bones, fortified soy milk, tofu and sesame spread through every day.
howItWorks:
**Calcium without dairy.** Fortified soy milk, greens, sesame, a little tofu, and sardines or small dried anchovies eaten with their soft bones add up through every day, never in one big glass. The week counts tofu at about 10% DV calcium on the label, so any tofu works. You don't need a calcium supplement; if you take one, ask your pharmacist whether you still need it.

**Vitamin D, B12 and soy.** Salmon, mackerel and sardines through the week, plus eggs and the soy milk, add **vitamin D, B12 and omega-3**. Vitamin D is hard to get from food alone: Health Canada advises 400 IU a day for adults over 50, and your care provider can say if you need one. If you take thyroid medication, ask your pharmacist whether to space it from soy foods.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's braised beef and tofu, Wednesday's rice plate, Thursday's mackerel, Friday's sundubu and Saturday's dumplings each make two portions for the next meal. Dumplings are the weekend project, and make Tuesday's iriko a double batch and it covers Friday's snack too.

**Brown rice batches.** Cook three pots just before you need them. Standard: about 2 cups dry on Sunday, 1 on Wednesday and 1 on Friday (1 cup dry makes about 3 cups cooked). Light needs a little less, Big about one and a half times. Cool hot rice in trays under 5 cm deep within 1 hour, eat within 3 days, and rinse it before cooking.

**Salt and sizes.** Reduced-sodium soy sauce, a little miso, kimchi and chili bean paste do most of the seasoning, in small amounts, with iodized salt as the salt. Light covers 1600-1800 only, with one snack a day. Big adds an extra snack on four days and bigger portions of rice and protein.

name: East African Highlands & Coast (Light)
summary: A week of East African home cooking: misir wot and shiro on injera, a slow Saturday doro wat, Kenyan githeri and sukuma wiki, a Swahili mackerel curry and Somali suqaar. Teff, millet, sorghum and dried maize carry the grains, with greens and tomato every day and legumes on six.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's misir wot, Tuesday's githeri, Thursday's shiro, Friday's suqaar and Saturday's doro wat each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Tuesday's uji covers Wednesday's breakfast too.

**Fatty fish four times.** Mackerel on Wednesday, sardines on Sunday and sardine snacks on Tuesday and Thursday give you most of the week's **omega-3 and B12**, and help with vitamin D. The mackerel and Sunday's sardines are never leftovers, and the soft sardine bones add calcium.

**Teff, millet, sorghum and maize.** Injera is teff, rich in **iron and fibre**, so check the label for 100% teff. Millet makes the uji, sorghum goes under the suqaar and dried maize goes into the githeri. Soak the maize and beans on Monday night and pressure-cook them on Tuesday; the pot covers Tuesday's dinner and Wednesday's lunch.

**Spices with purpose.** Berbere flavours the wots, and niter kibbeh adds its butter and spice in small amounts. Chicken liver in the suqaar brings **choline and iron**, and kachumbari, basbaas and lemon keep every plate bright.

**Prep ahead.** Buy injera at an Ethiopian grocery and freeze it in portions. Cook Tuesday's uji on Monday evening while the misir wot simmers, boil Thursday's ful egg on Wednesday night, and roast the kolo mix on Wednesday while the sweet potato roasts. Cook the sorghum on Thursday evening while the shiro simmers.

name: Eastern European & Georgian Table (Light)
summary: A week at an Eastern European and Georgian table: kasha with mushrooms, borscht, gołąbki, lobio and a weekend satsivi, with herring, smoked sprats and trout for the fish, plus rye bread, kefir, pickles and herbs by the handful.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's borscht, Tuesday's lobio, Wednesday's gołąbki, Thursday's chicken with kasha, Friday's pasulj and Saturday's satsivi each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already cooked. Saturday's syrniki do the same for Sunday breakfast.

**Fish four times.** Pickled herring on Monday, smoked sprats on rye on Wednesday and Friday, and baked trout on Sunday carry your **omega-3 and B12**, and the herring and trout bring most of the week's vitamin D. The walnuts in the lobio, satsivi and pkhali add plant omega-3. Fish is always fresh or opened that day, never a leftover.

**Beans, buckwheat and rye.** White and red beans turn up in the borscht, lobio and pasulj, with buckwheat, barley and rye alongside. Together they **carry** your iron, folate, magnesium and fibre, and the peppers, cabbage and pomegranate bring vitamin C to help your body use the iron.

**Calcium, choline and a little liver.** Kefir, tvorog, sulguni, poppy seeds and the soft bones in sprats bring the **calcium**. name: Endurance Kitchen (Standard)
summary: A carb-first week of real home cooking for runners, cyclists and triathletes: ugali with beef stew, salmon rice bowls, chicken in salsa verde, sardine spaghetti and polenta ragu. Rice, pasta, oats, potatoes, bread, fruit and juice sit around your sessions, with protein at every meal and a recovery snack.
howItWorks:
**Carbs around your training.** Carbs sit at every meal, from rice, pasta, oats, potatoes, bread, ugali and polenta, with fruit and juice around them, so fuel is on the plate whenever your session falls. No schedule is assumed. In the week table the first snack is the pre-training one and the second is the recovery one. Move them to wherever they fit your day.

**Recovery.** Protein is spread over four eating times: breakfast, lunch, dinner and a recovery snack that pairs carbs with protein, like chocolate milk, yogurt with mango or an egg sandwich. Eat it within an hour or two of finishing. Beef is on the plate twice, with beans and greens, and the salmon and sardines land on day 2 and day 4.

**Hydration and salt.** Drink water through the day, more in the heat, and to thirst during sessions. Salty foods such as miso, soy sauce, sardines and the salted potatoes are welcome, within the app's sodium ceiling. For sessions over about 90 minutes, a sports drink or gel is an easy extra, but none are in the recipes.

**Cook once, eat twice.** The day 1 beef stew, day 3 chicken, day 5 turkey and day 6 ragu each make two portions, so the next lunch is done. Fish is cooked fresh. Wash vegetables, herbs and fruit before cutting, and chill leftovers within 2 hours (1 hour for rice and grains).

**Big and XL.** Rice, pasta, ugali, oats, potatoes and bread grow the most, with more protein alongside, and some days gain an extra snack, such as arroz con leche. Vegetables and fruit stay as written, so the bigger plates are bigger bowls of starch, not bigger salads.

name: Everyday Classics (Light)
summary: The easy default week most people would recognise: oatmeal and toast breakfasts, lemon chicken with brown rice, salmon with potatoes, whole-wheat spaghetti with lentil tomato sauce and bean soup with rye. Whole grains in modest portions beside plenty of vegetables and legumes.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's bean soup, Tuesday's lemon chicken and rice, Wednesday's lentil spaghetti, Thursday's chili and Saturday's roast chicken each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. Cool the rice and spaghetti portions within an hour.

**Fish and beans.** Salmon sandwich on Monday, baked salmon on Friday and baked trout on Sunday, plus canned-salmon toasts as snacks, bring omega-3 and some **vitamin D**, which is hard to get from food alone. Fish is never a leftover. One can covers Monday's sandwich and Tuesday's toast, and another covers Wednesday and Thursday. Beans, lentils or chickpeas turn up most days.

**Whole grains, kept modest.** Oatmeal, whole-wheat toast, rye, brown rice and whole-wheat pasta stay in fist-sized portions, always next to vegetables and beans.

**Eggs on four days.** Choline is hard to reach without them, so scrambled eggs open Monday, Tuesday, Friday and Saturday. At Light, where the chicken portions are smaller, a hard-boiled egg on rye joins Wednesday and Thursday as a snack. Swap in tofu or more chicken if you prefer, though they bring less choline than eggs.

**Easy week.** Weekday dinners take 45 to 50 minutes start to finish, most of it simmering or roasting while you do something else. Saturday's roast is the slower tray, and Sunday's trout takes under 40. Wash produce, use a thermometer, and cook eggs until the yolk is firm.

**Sizes.** Light (1600 to 1800) has smaller portions of chicken, beef, grains, potatoes, bread, oil and cheese, and a little less of the beans and canned salmon; the vegetables, lentils and fish dinners stay about the same. It stops at 1600 because Saturday and Sunday can't shrink further and keep every nutrient. Big adds a snack on four days and a little more of everything else.

name: Family Kitchen (Light)
summary: A mild, generous family week: tacos with the toppings on the table, a pasta bake with the vegetables blended into the sauce, baked salmon fish fingers, salmon rice bowls, a gentle chicken soup and a Saturday pizza night. Adult portions, kid-approved flavours, and a vegetable in every dish.
howItWorks:
**Mild in the pot, heat on the table.** Nothing here is cooked spicy. Adults add hot sauce, pickled jalapeños or chili flakes at the table. Every main dish carries vegetables, grated into the taco filling or blended into the pasta sauce. Tell the kids what is in it, let them grate and stir, and keep raw vegetables on the table too.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's tacos, Wednesday's pasta bake, Friday's soup and Saturday's pizza each make two portions, so the next lunch is done. Egg muffins cover Tuesday and Wednesday breakfasts. The fish fingers, rice bowls and sheet-pan chicken are cooked fresh. Pizza night is the slow one, so make the dough in the morning.

**Omega-3, iron and calcium.** Salmon fish fingers on Tuesday and salmon rice bowls on Thursday carry your omega-3, with a little ground flax in the oatmeal and smoothies. Beans, turkey, chicken, edamame and spinach bring iron, with tomatoes, peppers and broccoli for vitamin C. Yogurt, milk and a little cheese bring calcium.

**What changes at each size.** Standard is the plan as written. Light shrinks the grains, protein and fats, keeps the vegetables, and drops the second snack Monday to Saturday. It starts at 1,600 kcal, because these family dishes do not shrink to 1,400 and stay nutritious. Big adds a snack every day.

**Little ones.** Set a baby's portion aside before any salt, maple syrup, soy sauce or glaze goes in. Offer cow's milk as a drink from 9 to 12 months, and keep to whole (3.25%) milk and yogurt until age 2. Cut grapes and cherry tomatoes in quarters, and skip whole nuts under 4.

name: Fish and Seafood Week (Light)
summary: Fish or seafood at dinner six nights, all low in mercury: sheet-pan salmon, trout with lentils, a shrimp and white bean skillet, mackerel on potato salad, cod and chickpea stew, and mussels in tomato broth. Four dishes make tomorrow's lunch, and beans, vegetables, eggs and nuts fill in the rest.
howItWorks:
**Fish most days.** Salmon on Monday, trout on Tuesday, shrimp on Wednesday, mackerel on Thursday, cod on Friday and mussels on Saturday, plus canned salmon in Sunday's lunch. Salmon, trout, mackerel and canned salmon bring **omega-3 and vitamin D**. Shrimp, cod and mussels add lean protein, iodine and B12. All of it is low in mercury.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's salmon tray, Wednesday's lentil soup, Thursday's mackerel potato salad and Friday's cod stew each make two portions. Cooked fish keeps up to 2 days, so each second portion is the very next lunch, cold or reheated once until steaming (74 °C). Mussels are cooked and eaten the same day.

**Not only fish.** Sunday's dinner is a black bean and sweet potato chili, and lentils, chickpeas, white beans or edamame turn up most days. Eggs cooked firm cover three breakfasts and two snack plates, and nuts or seeds land every day for crunch and magnesium.

**Easy on salt.** Beans are no-salt-added, feta is a garnish, and the broths and stews get their flavour from tomato, fennel, lemon, garlic and herbs. Wash all fruit and vegetables before cutting, lemons too. No fresh tuna, swordfish or shark appears.

**What changes with size.** Light covers 1,400 to 1,800 kcal. The fresh fish and eggs stay at or near full size, while the canned salmon, quinoa, oats, potatoes, oil, nuts and some beans shrink, and a snack drops on five days. At 1,400 the grains and potatoes are a small side. Big grows the fish, potatoes and beans and adds a snack on three days.

name: Gluten-free Latin Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Latin American home cooking that is gluten-free because the cuisine is: Colombian arepas and ajiaco, Peruvian quinoa soup and salmon in ají amarillo, Brazilian galinhada and moqueca, and Mexican tacos and weekend tamales. Corn, rice, quinoa, potato, cassava and plantain take turns, with lime, cilantro and chile throughout.
howItWorks:
**Gluten-free by its ingredients.** Nothing here is a substitute: corn, rice, quinoa, potato, cassava, plantain and tapioca take turns. If you have celiac disease, check that tortillas say 100% corn, and buy masarepa, masa harina and tapioca starch from a gluten-free line. Stock, chipotles in adobo, colorau and spice blends are where hidden gluten hides.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's quinoa soup, Thursday's galinhada and Saturday's tamales each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. Wednesday evening's quinoa con leche covers both Thursday and Friday breakfasts.

**Fish four times.** Salmon on Tuesday and Friday, sardines in Thursday's causa and a quick sardine plate on Sunday carry your **omega-3** and **vitamin D**, and the soft sardine bones add calcium. Flaxseed in the yogurt bowls and chia in the chía fresca add a little more omega-3 through the week.

**Sunday bean pot.** Soak about 2 cups of dried black beans overnight, then simmer them with an onion and a bay leaf for about 1 hour, salting at the end. That's enough for the week. They keep 4 to 5 days, so freeze a tub. Rice keeps 3 days, so cook it close to the day.

**Eggs, dairy and greens.** Eggs carry **choline**, and so do beef, chicken and a little liver. Queijo coalho, yogurt and milk carry calcium, and kale, spinach and beans carry **iron and folate** most days.

name: Gluten-free Mediterranean (Light)

howItWorks:
**Gluten-free by its ingredients.** Buckwheat, potatoes, rice, cornmeal, chickpea flour and beans have always carried this cuisine, so most of it needs no substitute. Stock, polenta, chickpea flour, buckwheat and spice blends can hide wheat or share a mill, so if you have celiac disease, buy sealed packs marked gluten-free.

name: Gluten-free South Asian (Light)
summary: A week of South Asian home cooking that is gluten-free because the cuisine is: idli and sambar, besan chilla, jowar bhakri, Kerala fish and a weekend chicken biryani. Rice, millets, dals and coconut take turns, with fish three times.
howItWorks:
**Gluten-free by its ingredients.** Rice, besan, jowar, millet, cassava and dal do the work, so the week is mostly naturally gluten-free. If you have celiac disease, buy besan, jowar flour, rice flour and millets in sealed gluten-free-marked packs. Check the label on hing (usually cut with wheat), sambar powder, chaat masala, garam masala, ground chili and turmeric.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's Kolhapuri chicken, Wednesday's kadhi khichdi, Friday's kadala curry and Saturday's biryani each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Saturday's idlis cover Sunday breakfast too.

**Fish three times.** Goan mackerel on Tuesday, Kerala sardines on Thursday and Sri Lankan salmon on Sunday carry your **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**. None are back to back, and all are cooked fresh.

**Prep ahead.** On Thursday night, soak about 1¼ cups of kala chana (brown chickpeas). Cook them all on Friday for the kadala curry and keep the rest for the weekend's sundal and roasted chickpeas. On Friday morning, soak the rice and urad for Saturday's idlis and grind them that evening.

**Eggs, dairy and greens.** Eggs turn up every day, boiled as a snack, in the egg roast and bhurji and on the biryani, and with dal, moong, chicken and fish they carry **choline**. Milk, yogurt and chaas carry calcium, with sesame in the chutneys and bhakri. Kale, peas and chickpeas bring iron and folate. Coconut is used by the spoonful, so saturated fat stays within 10%.

name: Gulf Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Gulf home cooking: chicken machboos, lamb saloona, beef and okra marag, grilled kanaad with dakkous, roasted sardines and a slow Saturday lamb harees. Brown basmati, whole-wheat khubz and legumes, with dates, laban and nuts for snacks.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's machboos, Wednesday's saloona, Thursday's marag and Saturday's harees each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. Pack the rice or bread with it.

**Fish twice, plus shrimp.** Kanaad with dakkous on Tuesday and fresh sardines on Friday carry your **omega-3 and vitamin D**. Both are cooked fresh, three days apart, and shrimp rounds out Sunday.

**Whole grains the Gulf way.** Brown basmati in the machboos, marag and shrimp, whole-wheat khubz, and cracked wheat in the harees. Dates are a small sweetness, one or two at a time, so the **glycaemic load** stays in check.

**Breakfasts that rotate.** Foul, balaleet-inspired vermicelli and tomato eggs each come round two or three times, never on back-to-back mornings. The eggs and fava beans carry your **choline and a good share of your iron**, and laban or milk snacks keep **calcium** up.

**Weekend project.** Saturday's harees is mostly hands-off simmering. Cooking fats are the Gulf kitchen's own, vegetable oil and a little ghee, with olive oil for salads and the nakhi.

name: Gut Health Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of fibre-rich home cooking from Korea, Germany, the Mediterranean, India and Japan: beans and lentils, oats, barley and rye, lots of vegetables and a fermented food every day, with more than 30 different plant foods.
howItWorks:
**More than 30 plant foods a week.** The idea is variety: lots of different vegetables, fruit, beans, whole grains, nuts and seeds across the week, not a big pile of one. Shiitake, kale, kimchi cabbage, lentils, barley, rye, hazelnuts and raspberries all turn up, so every meal brings something different.

**A fermented food every day.** Kefir, yogurt, miso, kimchi and sauerkraut turn up daily inside real dishes, as food rather than medicine. Buy kimchi and sauerkraut from the refrigerated section and look for "live" or "unpasteurised" on the label, since shelf-stable jars are heat-treated. Kimchi often contains fish sauce or shrimp, so check the label. Stir miso in off the boil.

**Fibre, calcium and iron.** This week is high in fibre, and Big is a lot of it. If you usually eat less, start with half the beans and lentils for the first week or two and drink water through the day. The food also brings plenty of calcium and a good amount of iron, so don't add a calcium or iron supplement unless your care team advises it.

**Salt and the Sunday batch.** Kimchi, sauerkraut and miso are salty, so each recipe measures them, the beans are no-salt-added, and lemon, vinegar and herbs do the brightening. On Sunday cook brown rice and pearl barley (amounts are in the jjigae tip) and cool them within an hour. Keep Monday to Wednesday's portions in the fridge and freeze the rest, thawing in the fridge overnight and using within 2 days.

**Light and Big.** Light has one snack a day and trims the grains, protein, nuts and oil, with a fermented food still in every day. Big adds a third snack and bigger portions.

name: Healthy Ageing 60+ (Light)
summary: Soft, flavourful food for one or two from Canadian, Mediterranean, Japanese and British kitchens: 25 g or more of protein at every meal, fish through the week, and stews and soups that freeze in single portions.
howItWorks:
**Protein at every meal.** Eggs, milk, Greek yogurt, fish, chicken, lamb, beef, tofu and lentils put a solid portion of protein on every breakfast, lunch and dinner, and the snacks add a little more. Steady protein at each meal helps look after muscle.

**Calcium, vitamin D and B12.** Milk, yogurt, calcium-set tofu, and canned salmon and sardines with their soft bones bring the calcium. Salmon, mackerel, sardines, eggs and Canadian milk (fortified with vitamin D) bring D. B12 comes from fish, eggs, dairy and meat. The week already brings most days' calcium from food, so check with your care team before adding a calcium pill on top.

**Soft on purpose.** Porridge, braises, stews, soups, creamy eggs, mash and flaky baked fish can all be eaten with a spoon or a fork. Lentils melt, spinach wilts and vegetables cook until tender. Salt is kept in check with herbs, lemon, ginger and tomato.

**Cook for one or two.** Lentil soup, shepherd's pie, niku-dofu, the chicken braise and the haddock chowder each make two portions: eat one, chill the other for tomorrow. The soup, pie and braise freeze well: cool single portions fully, freeze, then thaw in the fridge and use within 2 days. Fatty fish is always cooked fresh, and the niku-dofu and chowder stay in the fridge rather than the freezer.

**Light size.** Light drops the second snack and uses fewer lentils in the soup, less chicken in the braise, less rice with the mackerel and a little less oil; fish, eggs, tofu, beef and lamb stay the same, so every meal keeps its protein. Light covers 1600-1800 only; a lower band could not keep calcium, vitamin E and protein at every meal.

name: Heart-healthy Asian (Light)
summary: A week of bright, fragrant Asian home cooking built to stay low in sodium and saturated fat: brown rice, tofu and edamame, fish three times, and ginger, garlic, scallion, lime and chili doing the seasoning. Soy sauce, miso and fish sauce are kept to teaspoons, so it still tastes full.
howItWorks:
**Flavour without the salt.** Ginger, garlic, scallion, lemongrass, lime, rice vinegar, chili, sesame, star anise and cilantro do most of the seasoning. Soy sauce, miso and fish sauce stay in the dishes, but as teaspoons, and always paired with acid or heat.

**Fish, soy and whole grains.** Salmon on Tuesday, mackerel on Thursday and trout on Sunday bring omega-3, and they're always cooked fresh. Tofu, edamame and soy milk carry plant protein, while brown rice, barley, oats and buckwheat soba keep the starch mostly whole-grain. Cook a double pot of rice and barley on Sunday and keep it 4 days; freeze the rest.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's shrimp and tofu, Wednesday's tofu stir-fry, Friday's tofu stew and Saturday's pho each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. At Light the second snack drops and there's a little less oil and noodles, while the fish and tofu stay the same; at Big a snack is added each day.

**Shop for low sodium.** Choose reduced-sodium soy sauce, low-sodium broth, calcium-set firm tofu, plain peeled shrimp and unsalted peanuts, and cook noodles in unsalted water. Fish sauce and miso are a splash, not a pour.

**A note on your care team.** If you take blood-pressure or heart medication, follow your care team's advice. This plan is just built to be low in sodium and saturated fat.

**A note on your care team.** If you take blood-pressure or heart medication, follow your care team's advice. This plan is just built to be low in sodium and saturated fat.

name: DASH North American (Light)
summary: A week of hearty North American home cooking built around fruit, vegetables, beans, fish, low-fat dairy and unsalted nuts, with lots of flavour from citrus, vinegar, garlic, herbs and spice instead of salt. Chili, sheet-pan chicken, fish tacos and a Sunday roast, all low in sodium and saturated fat.
howItWorks:
**Flavour without the salt.** Lime, lemon and cider vinegar brighten most dishes. Garlic, onion, ancho chile and smoked paprika add depth, and roasting browns the edges. Six dishes get a pinch of salt, and that's all the salt in the week.

**Fruit, vegetables and the DASH way.** Fruit starts every breakfast, vegetables fill lunches and dinners, and there's low-fat milk or yogurt every day. Beans, oats, brown rice, unsalted nuts, potatoes, sweet potatoes and bananas bring potassium and fibre.

**Fish, and cook once, eat twice.** Seared salmon on Monday, almond-crusted trout on Wednesday and salmon tacos on Saturday bring omega-3, always cooked fresh. Monday's chili, Tuesday's chicken, Thursday's apple-sage chicken and Friday's red beans each make two portions, so the next lunch is done.

**Pick no-salt-added cans.** Look for "no salt added" on canned beans and tomatoes, "low sodium" on broth and "reduced sodium" on bread, and rinse beans anyway. Buy unsalted nuts.

**Light and Big.** The second snack drops away at Light, portions are smaller and there's less rice and tortilla. At Big the dishes grow and the snacks stay the same. If you take blood-pressure or heart medication, follow your care team's advice.

name: Heart-healthy Mediterranean (Light)
summary: A week of bright, lemony Mediterranean cooking built to stay low in sodium and saturated fat: oats and walnuts, beans and lentils, oily fish three times, and olive oil everywhere. The flavour comes from lemon, vinegar, garlic, herbs and spice, not the salt shaker.
howItWorks:
**Flavour without the salt.** Lemon, red wine and sherry vinegar, garlic, oregano, sumac, smoked paprika and fresh herbs do the seasoning, and a splash of acid at the end is what makes a dish taste finished. Salt is only a pinch, in the soup, stews, chicken and fish.

**Fish, beans, oats and olive oil.** Salmon on Tuesday, fresh sardines on Thursday and trout on Sunday bring omega-3, and they're never leftovers. Legumes turn up most days, oats and walnuts start three mornings, and olive oil is the main fat.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's lemon chicken, Wednesday's lentil soup, Friday's chickpea and spinach stew and Saturday's stuffed peppers each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done.

**Pick no-salt-added cans.** Check the label for "no salt added" on beans, chickpeas, lentils, tomatoes and tuna, and rinse beans anyway. Buy unsalted nuts, and keep feta to a sprinkle.

**A note on your care team.** If you take blood-pressure or heart medication, follow your care team's advice. This plan is just built to be low in sodium and saturated fat.

name: Iron Focus (Light)
summary: A week built to reach 18 mg of iron every day from real food: lean beef and lamb, sardines, mussels and mackerel, lentils, chickpeas and beans, tofu, pumpkin seeds and greens, each with vitamin C on the plate.
howItWorks:
**Two kinds of iron.** Heme iron, from red meat and fish, is absorbed easily, and mussels are rich in iron too. Plant iron, from lentils, beans, tofu and seeds, is absorbed less well, but there is plenty of it here.

**Vitamin C at every iron meal.** Vitamin C helps your body take up plant iron, so peppers, tomatoes, citrus, broccoli, strawberries and lemon sit right beside the lentils, beans and tofu. The tomato and lemon do the same job in the dal.

**Tea and coffee between meals.** Tea and coffee hold back iron absorption when drunk with a meal, so none are in these recipes. Have yours an hour or two before or after eating, mid-morning or mid-afternoon.

**Calcium in its place.** Calcium competes with iron on the same plate, so yogurt mostly lives at the snacks, with just a few spoonfuls on the bran bowl. Dairy still adds up to a good part of your calcium over the day.

**Fish and leftovers.** Sardines on Tuesday and Friday and mackerel on Sunday give the omega-3, with mussels on Thursday. Monday, Wednesday, Friday and Saturday dinners make two portions for the next day's lunch. At Light, which starts at 1,600 kcal, the second snack drops away and the meals stay about the same size.

name: Filipino, Malaysian & Indonesian Table (Light)
summary: A week of Filipino, Malaysian and Indonesian home cooking: bubur ayam, nasi lemak and tapsilog breakfasts, chicken adobo, mackerel sinigang, pinakbet, a lighter beef rendang, gado-gado, a laksa-inspired weekend soup and grilled mackerel with sambal, all on brown rice.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Tuesday's adobo, Wednesday's tempeh stir-fry, Thursday's pinakbet, Friday's rendang and Saturday's laksa each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. The kacang hijau makes two bowls too. The mackerel is always cooked fresh.

**Rice batch.** On Sunday, cook 1½ cups of dry brown rice (about 4½ cups cooked) for Monday to Wednesday, and simmer Monday's bubur base while you're at it. On Wednesday night, cook another 1½ cups dry (about 4½ cups cooked) for Thursday to Sunday. It keeps 4 or 5 days in the fridge. Press a little into a block on Sunday for Monday's gado-gado.

**Fish four times.** Mackerel sinigang on Monday, sardine sambal on Wednesday and Friday and mackerel ikan bakar on Sunday bring your **omega-3**, and the sardine bones bring calcium. None of them land on back-to-back days.

**Coconut as flavour.** Coconut milk goes in by the spoonful, for the nasi lemak rice, the rendang, the laksa and the kacang hijau. The cooking oil is canola, in small amounts, so **saturated fat stays under 10%**.

**Salt, and a little liver.** Soy sauce, fish sauce and shrimp paste do most of the salting, plus a measured pinch of salt, and each recipe measures them. A little chicken liver in the bubur ayam, as many Jakarta cooks do, brings **vitamin A, B12 and choline**.

name: Japanese & Korean Home Table (Light)
summary: A week at the Japanese and Korean home table: miso soup, grilled fish, soba, rice bowls, namul and a hot pot, with brown rice and barley, tofu and plenty of vegetables.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's teriyaki, Wednesday's jjigae and Saturday's bibimbap each make two portions, so Tuesday, Thursday and Sunday lunches are done. The banchan and the dak-juk are also made once for two breakfasts.

**Sunday prep.** Cook a big pot of brown rice and pearl barley, portion it, and cook a second batch on Wednesday night. It keeps four days, so every rice meal is a quick reheat. Roast a tray of sweet potatoes and make a jar of nut jorim too.

**Fish three times.** Salmon on Tuesday, mackerel on Thursday and a quick salmon soba on Saturday bring your **omega-3 and vitamin D**, never two days in a row. Walnuts in the snacks and the porridge add more.

**Soy, seaweed and noodles.** Tofu, natto, edamame and the bean pastes carry protein, and calcium-set tofu carries calcium. Nori and wakame add iodine. Soba and udon take turns with the rice so the week never turns into a rice wall.

**Saturday is the long day.** Dak-juk in the morning and bibimbap at night take the most time, so weeknights stay quick. Miso, tamari and kimchi bring the salt, so each recipe measures them and lets ginger, vinegar and mandarin add the brightness.

name: Keto Asian (Light)
summary: A week of grilled fish, stir-fries, a green curry, a Korean lettuce-wrap spread and a hot pot, with no rice, noodles or sugar. Net carbs stay at 40 g or less every day, and the fat comes from fish, avocado, nuts, sesame and a little coconut.
howItWorks:
**Where the carbs went.** There is no rice, noodle or sugar here. Cauliflower rice stands in once, lettuce wraps the beef, and with no sugar the flavour comes from garlic, chili, sesame and fermented pastes. Greens, mushrooms and tofu fill the plate, so net carbs stay under the keto ceiling every day.

**Fat from fish, nuts and avocado.** Salmon, mackerel, avocado, walnuts, pumpkin seeds and sesame carry the calories. Canola does the frying, with perilla or sesame oil to finish. Coconut is light and shows up only in the green curry and the tom yum, so saturated fat stays under 10%.

**Fatty fish three times.** Salmon on Tuesday and Saturday mornings and mackerel on Thursday night bring **omega-3 and vitamin D**, never on back-to-back days. Sea bass in Friday's tom yum and Sunday's hot pot is the lean fish. Perilla oil, walnuts and fish carry the omega-3 that balances the sesame.

**Greens carry the vitamins.** Spinach, bok choy, gai lan or lettuce is at nearly every meal for **folate, vitamin C, vitamin K and potassium**. Calcium-set tofu, gai lan and bok choy do the calcium work without dairy, pumpkin seeds add magnesium, chicken and sesame add B vitamins, and a few clams in Monday's stew add a big hit of B12.

**Cook once, eat twice.** The curry, mapo tofu, ginger chicken, bulgogi wraps and krapow each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Sunday's hot pot is a one-pot finish. Doubanjiang, gochujang and doenjang usually contain wheat, so anyone avoiding gluten should look for gluten-free versions, and check the miso and kimchi labels too.

name: Keto Latin (Light)
summary: Carne asada with nopales, Peruvian ceviche and trout, chicken fajita bowls, camarones a la diabla, a weekend steak with chimichurri and a Brazilian moqueca, all very low in carbs. Avocado, nuts and seeds, olive oil and fish carry the fat, and salsas and vegetables carry the vitamins.
howItWorks:
**Avocado, nuts, seeds and fish carry the fat.** Avocado at most meals, pecans, almonds and toasted pepitas, olive oil in the chimichurri, and trout and sardines do the work. There is no cheese or cream, and the coconut milk is light, so saturated fat stays under 10%.

**Where the carbs went.** No tortillas, rice, beans, corn or plantain. Lettuce cups and cucumber do the scooping, cauliflower stands in for rice, and onion, tomato and lime are measured like seasoning. Net carbs stay under the keto limit every day, at every size.

**Salsas and vegetables carry the vitamins.** Nopales, tomatillo salsa verde, peppers, spinach and collards bring **vitamin A, vitamin C, folate and calcium**. Pepitas and chia add magnesium, pepitas and sunflower seeds bring thiamin, and sardines with their soft bones add more calcium.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's carne asada, Wednesday's fajita bowls, Friday's achiote chicken and Saturday's steak each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Soak two chia jars on Sunday and blend Monday's ancho paste the night before, then rub it on the steak when you get home.

**Fatty fish twice.** Trout on Tuesday and sardines on Friday carry the omega-3 and **vitamin D**, never back to back. Chia pudding and chía fresca add plant omega-3 on the other days.

name: Keto Mediterranean (Light)

name: Keto Middle Eastern (Light)
summary: A week of Lebanese, Syrian, Turkish and Gulf flavours without the bread, rice or sugar: shawarma bowls, kofta, baba ghanoush, samke harra and shakshuka. Net carbs stay at 40 g or less every day, and the fat comes from olive oil, avocado, nuts, tahini and fish rather than cheese or cream.
howItWorks:
**Where the carbs went.** There is no bread, rice, bulgur or sugar here. Cauliflower stands in for the grain in tabbouleh and machboos, lettuce for the flatbread, and tomato, onion, garlic and lemon are measured like seasoning. Every day stays under the net-carb ceiling at every size.

**Fat from the pantry.** Olive oil, avocado, olives, tahini and fish carry the calories, with walnuts and hazelnuts used the way Turkish and Syrian cooks use them: in sauces, dips and fillings, over the machboos, and toasted as a snack. Labneh and yogurt are small, and lamb appears only in the weekend kofta, so saturated fat stays under 10% of calories.

**Fatty fish three times.** Anchovies on Tuesday, sardines on Friday and trout on Sunday carry the omega-3, and walnuts add a little plant omega-3 on the days between. The sardines are eaten with their soft bones, which makes Friday the big **calcium** day. Sea bass on Thursday is a fourth, leaner fish.

**Greens do the vitamin work.** Kale, spinach, romaine, arugula, parsley and cilantro turn up at almost every meal, with eggplant and cauliflower for bulk. They bring **calcium, vitamin A, folate and fibre**, a spoon of chia in the labneh plate adds more fibre, and an egg at every breakfast helps with choline.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's Circassian chicken, Wednesday's stuffed eggplant, Friday's shawarma bowls and Saturday's kofta each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. On the Sunday before, roast the eggplant halves for Wednesday and toast a jar of hazelnuts.

name: Lean Asian (Light)
summary: Big, bright bowls and plates from Vietnam, Japan, Korea, Thailand and China: herb-heaped chicken pho, a grilled mackerel set meal, soft tofu stew, larb in lettuce cups and steamed fish with greens. It is real home cooking, built to keep you full on fewer calories.
howItWorks:
**Protein at every meal.** Chicken, beef, shrimp, salmon, eggs, tofu, edamame and Greek yogurt carry real protein, the most filling thing on the plate. A smaller meal still feels like a proper one.

**Volume first.** Broths, herbs, sprouts, napa cabbage, mushrooms, cucumber and greens fill the bowl, and edamame and tofu bring the fibre. Rice and noodles stay as modest scoops beside them.

**Fatty fish three times.** Canned salmon on Monday, grilled mackerel on Wednesday and a salmon miso hot pot on Friday carry the omega-3 and some vitamin D. Steamed sea bass on Sunday keeps it lean. A few drops of toasted perilla oil, the nutty Korean finishing oil, add plant omega-3 on most days.

**Flavour without the salt.** Lime, chili, ginger, vinegar, herbs and toasted rice powder carry the taste. Reduced-sodium soy sauce, fish sauce and miso go in by the teaspoon, so the food is properly seasoned and the sodium stays sensible.

**Cook once, eat twice.** The pho, tofu stew, larb, nabe and braise each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. At Light, the rice, noodles, oil, yogurt, chicken and most of the tofu shrink, Friday has no snack and the weekend one each, and the vegetables, fish, shrimp, beef and eggs barely move.

name: Lean Global Kitchen (Light)
summary: Big, bright plates from Mexico, Japan, China, the US and Italy: turkey chili, burrito bowls on greens, miso soup with tofu, shrimp and soba, and a shrimp stir-fry piled with vegetables. It is real home cooking, built to keep you full on fewer calories.
howItWorks:
**Protein at every meal.** Turkey, chicken, shrimp, tofu, yogurt, cottage cheese and eggs carry real protein, and fish three times (canned salmon Monday, salmon Wednesday, sardines Sunday) adds omega-3 and helps with vitamin D. Protein is the most filling thing on the plate, so a smaller meal still feels like a proper one.

**Volume and fibre first.** Big salads, crunchy cabbage, a bowl of miso soup, greens and a pot of chili with mushrooms stirred in fill the plate. Beans, edamame or chickpeas turn up every day, with a little hominy, so you get **plenty of fibre** and feel full before the food runs out.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's chili, Tuesday's miso soup, Thursday's burrito bowls, Friday's stir-fry and Saturday's chicken pozole each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done.

**Flavour without fuss.** Lime, smoked paprika, ginger, miso, soy, lemon and oregano do the work, so nothing tastes like diet food.

**What Light changes.** Vegetables never shrink, and the turkey, chicken, shrimp, fish, eggs and breakfast yogurt barely move. Light trims the rice, soba, hominy, toast, oil and almonds, and some of the chicken, tofu, beans and cottage cheese. It keeps one snack a day.

name: Lean Mediterranean (Light)
summary: Big salads, brothy soups and roasted vegetables from Greece, Italy and Spain, built around lean protein, beans and plenty of fibre. It is generous Mediterranean food, built to keep you full on fewer calories.
howItWorks:
**Protein at every meal.** Chicken, cod, turkey, shrimp, chicken skewers, tuna, nonfat Greek yogurt and egg whites all carry real protein, and sardines on Friday and salmon on Sunday add omega-3 and vitamin D. Protein is the most filling thing on the plate, so a smaller meal still feels like a proper one.

**Volume and fibre first.** Big salads, fennel, cabbage, a brothy soup and a tray of roasted vegetables fill the plate, and white beans, chickpeas, lentils or lupini turn up every day. Together they bring **plenty of fibre** and take up room, so you feel full before the food runs out.

**Cook once, eat twice.** The Greek chicken salad, cod stew, keftedes, lentejas and souvlaki each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done, and the frittata covers Sunday's breakfast. On Friday night, marinate the pork for Saturday's souvlaki.

**Flavour without fuss.** Lemon, vinegar, oregano, capers, olives, smoked paprika and a little feta do the work, so nothing tastes like diet food.

**What Light changes.** Every meal keeps its vegetables, and the cod, turkey, shrimp, pork, tuna, sardines and salmon stay much the same. Light trims the pita, oil, feta, olives and walnuts, some of the beans, chicken, egg whites and breakfast yogurt, and keeps one snack a day. Each plate still looks like a meal.

name: Levantine Table (Standard)
summary: A week at a Levantine table. Foul, labneh and balila for breakfast, lentils, chickpeas and bulgur on most days, lamb and chicken in moderation, and fish three times. Lebanese, Syrian, Palestinian and Jordanian dishes, with sumac, za'atar, tahini and plenty of herbs.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's shish tawook, Tuesday's mujadara, Thursday's adas bi hamod and Saturday's kibbeh each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Saturday's ijjeh does the same for Sunday breakfast.

**Fish three times.** Salmon samke harra on Wednesday, sardines on Friday and mackerel on Sunday carry your **omega-3 and vitamin D**. They are never back to back, and always cooked fresh.

**Legumes most days.** Fava beans, chickpeas and lentils turn up at breakfast, lunch or dinner. With bulgur and whole-wheat pita they cover your **iron, folate and fibre**, and the lemon and tomato beside them help your body use the iron.

**Calcium the Levantine way.** Tahini, labneh, halloumi, yogurt, dried figs and the soft bones of canned sardines carry your **calcium**, with parsley and chard for vitamins K and C.

**Prep ahead.** The Sunday before, boil a few eggs for the week's breakfasts. On Thursday evening, while the soup simmers, make a batch of hummus for the Friday and Sunday snacks. Saturday's kibbeh is the weekend project, so soak the bulgur first and get the oven hot.

name: Diabetes-friendly Latin (Light)
summary: Diabetes-friendly Latin home cooking from Mexico, Central America, Peru, Colombia and the Caribbean: beans at most meals, one honest tortilla, arepa or spoonful of rice at a time, big salads and slaws, and fish or shrimp most days.
howItWorks:
**Steady carbs, three times a day.** Lunch and dinner each get one honest portion of starch, and most breakfasts do too: a corn tortilla, a small arepa, a little brown rice, quinoa, camote or plantain. It always sits beside beans, eggs, fish or chicken, so the starch digests more slowly.

**Beans and vegetables with every carb.** Black and pinto beans and chickpeas turn up at two meals on most days and carry the **fibre and protein**. Cabbage, radish, jícama, tomato and lettuce come with the plate, so the crunch comes first and the starch last.

**Why the tortillas are counted.** One tortilla is a real part of the day, so it is written into each recipe. On the Light size the tortillas, arepa, some of the chicken and a few bean portions get smaller, while the vegetables and salsa stay as written.

**Lime, salsa and fish.** Lime, vinegar and fresh salsas finish every plate, and a sour, spicy bite makes a small portion of starch feel complete. Mackerel on Tuesday and salmon on Friday bring **omega-3**, and canned sardines on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday add calcium.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Tinga, arroz con pollo, ropa vieja and Saturday's pozole each make two portions, so the next lunch is done. On Sunday, cook the quinoa, toast a jar of almonds and pepitas, and make the curtido.

name: Diabetes-friendly Mediterranean (Light)
summary: Diabetes-friendly home cooking from Greece, southern Italy, Spain and Crete: beans, lentils and chickpeas every day, big salads first, small portions of barley, farro, pasta and rye, and fresh or canned fish most days.
howItWorks:
**Steady carbs, three times a day.** Breakfast, lunch and dinner each get a small, honest portion of starch: a thin slice of rye, a few spoonfuls of barley or farro, a handful of whole-wheat pasta. It always sits next to beans, lentils, eggs, fish or chicken, so the starch digests more slowly.

**Legumes at most meals.** Lentils, chickpeas, white beans and lupini turn up at two meals on most days and carry the **fibre and protein**. Pasta e ceci has far more chickpea than pasta, and the orzotto is mostly chicken, mushrooms, broccoli and beans.

name: Diabetes-friendly South Asian (Light)
summary: Diabetes-friendly home cooking from Punjab, Gujarat, Kerala, Pakistan and Sri Lanka, built around dal, beans and vegetables, with small portions of roti, brown basmati, millet and barley. Steady carbs, plenty of fibre, fish twice and a weekend barley haleem.
howItWorks:
**Steady carbs, three times a day.** Each meal gets one modest portion of starch: one roti, a spoonful or two of brown basmati, or a little millet or barley. On the Light size these are small, a palm-sized roti or a spoonful of rice, and dal and vegetables fill the plate. It always comes with dal, beans, yogurt, fish or chicken, so the starch digests more slowly.

**Big dal, small rice, salad first.** Moong, toor, chana dal, rajma and chickpeas turn up at two meals on most days and carry **fibre and protein**. Kachumber, raita, thoran and mallung come with the meal, with lemon or tamarind for the sour. Eat the crunch first and the starch last.

**Fish on Tuesday and Friday.** Kerala-style mackerel curry and Sri Lankan pepper and tamarind salmon bring **omega-3** and vitamin D, and both are cooked fresh. Rajma, tuvar dal, the tandoori tray and Saturday's haleem each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done.

**Sunday prep.** Cook a pot of brown basmati for the first rice dinners and freeze a portion for Friday. Boil the week's eggs too. Soak the chana dal and millet on Wednesday and Saturday nights for the upma mornings, and the moong dal for each chilla morning.

**Eggs, curd and milk.** A boiled egg or an egg chaat turns up as a street snack on a few days and adds **choline and protein**. Curd, haldi doodh and paneer cover calcium and B12. Canola does the cooking, with just a spoonful of ghee on the dals and the haleem.

name: North African Spice Road (Light)
summary: A week on the North African spice road. Chakchouka, bissara and msemen for breakfast, a chicken and apricot tagine, harira, chermoula sardines, Algerian couscous and a slow lamb and prune tagine, with ras el hanout, harissa, preserved lemon and saffron throughout.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's chicken tagine, Tuesday's harira, Thursday's couscous and Saturday's lamb and prune tagine each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Tuesday evening's bissara pot also covers Wednesday and Thursday breakfasts. Pack the khobz or couscous separately.

**Fish most days.** Fresh sardines on Wednesday and harissa mackerel on Friday are the two fish dinners. Tinned mackerel, a sardine sandwich, sardine kefta and a tuna slata mechouia turn up at lunch and snack time, as they do in Moroccan and Tunisian kitchens, for **omega-3, calcium and vitamin D**.

**Legumes most days.** Fava in the bissara, lentils in the harira, and chickpeas in the tagines, couscous and snacks carry your **iron, folate and fibre**. The lemon, tomato and preserved lemon beside them help your body use the iron.

**Olive oil, whole grains and nuts.** Olive oil is the only cooking fat. Whole-wheat khobz and couscous replace the white ones, with oats and barley alongside. Almonds go in the tagines, and walnuts go with the dates.

**Prep ahead.** The Sunday before, toast a jar of almonds and walnuts for the porridge. Cook the bissara on Tuesday while the harira simmers, and make Saturday's zaalouk on Friday night. Saturday's lamb tagine is the slow project, and the msemen is the slow breakfast.

name: Mediterranean Coast (Light)
summary: A week of the way people eat along the Mediterranean coast: beans and lentils most days, olive oil, plenty of vegetables, oily fish twice plus shrimp, and a little feta and yogurt. Greek, Southern Italian and Spanish dishes built on potatoes, legumes, barley and oats.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's lemon chicken, Wednesday's lentil soup, Friday's chickpea stew and Saturday's saffron barley each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Saturday's tortilla also gives you a cold-slice breakfast on Sunday.

**Quick lunches.** A meze plate on Monday, a village salad on Wednesday and a Sicilian fava, orange and fennel salad on Friday come together in minutes.

**Fish three times.** Sardines on Tuesday, salmon on Thursday and shrimp on Sunday never land back to back, and are always cooked fresh. Sardines and salmon bring **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and the sardines' soft bones add calcium.

**Beans, eggs and greens.** Legumes show up most days and eggs every day, for **choline**. Kale, yogurt and feta cover calcium, and lentils, chickpeas and fava beans cover iron. Walnuts and a spoonful of chia in the oats balance the omega-6 from olive oil.

**Sunday prep.** Blitz a batch of hummus (it feeds Monday's meze plate and Thursday's snack) and mix the first jar of oats, then repeat on Tuesday and Thursday nights. Save your energy for **Saturday**, when the tortilla and saffron barley take more time.

name: Menopause Japanese (Light)
summary: A week of real Japanese home cooking: grilled and simmered fish, tofu, natto and edamame, small bowls of miso soup and barley rice. Built for women over 50, with plenty of calcium and 25 g or more of protein at every meal.
howItWorks:
**Calcium and protein.** Calcium-set tofu appears in most meals, joined by fortified soy milk, sesame, komatsuna, shirasu and the soft bones of canned salmon: about 1,000 to 1,800 mg of calcium a day from food. Every meal has a proper serving of protein. If you've had a hormone-sensitive cancer, ask your care team how much soy suits you.

**Fish, vitamin D and omega-3.** Salmon on Tuesday and Sunday and mackerel on Thursday, plus canned salmon on Monday, bring omega-3 and some vitamin D. A few drops of egoma (perilla) oil add plant omega-3 on the fish-free days. Vitamin D is still hard to get from food, so the note on this plan matters. Fish is always cooked fresh, never a leftover.

**Fibre and low-salt seasoning.** Mugi-gohan (rice cooked with pearled barley), oats, root vegetables, greens and edamame supply the fibre. Bonito and shiitake do the umami work, and reduced-sodium soy sauce and miso go in by the teaspoon. Seaweed is left out because kombu and wakame are very high in iodine.

**Iodine and vitamin K.** Iodine runs low on most days, with a light hand on salt and no seaweed. Iodized salt, fish and eggs give some, so ask your provider about a supplement. If you take warfarin, leave out the natto, which is very rich in a long-lasting form of vitamin K, and keep the leafy greens steady. Your care team can tell you more.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's hambagu, Wednesday's chikuzen-ni, Friday's sukiyaki and Saturday's gyoza each make two portions for the next day's lunch. At Light, the second snack drops away, the soba and gyoza wrappers shrink to about half, the rice gets a little smaller and the chikuzen-ni has less chicken, while the fish, tofu and eggs stay about the same.

name: Menopause Mediterranean (Light)
summary: A week of Greek, Italian and Spanish home cooking built for women over 50: calcium from yogurt, sardines and salmon with the bones, white beans, greens and tofu, and 25 g or more of protein at every meal.
howItWorks:
**Calcium all day.** Greek yogurt starts three mornings, and sardines and canned salmon (soft bones and all), white beans, kale, calcium-set tofu and fortified soy drink add more through the day. Food alone brings about **1,000 to 1,850 mg** a day here, so read the note before adding a calcium pill.

**Protein at every meal.** Eggs, yogurt, fish, chicken, turkey, beans and tofu give breakfast, lunch and dinner a solid protein portion, which helps look after muscle. Monday's soup and the Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday dinners each make an extra portion for the next day's lunch.

**Fish and vitamin D.** Salmon, sardines, mackerel and trout appear on most days, always made the day you eat them and never saved as a leftover, and bring omega-3 and a little vitamin D. Vitamin D is hard to get from food, so see the note about the daily supplement.

**Fibre and a heart-friendly plate.** Beans, lentils, chickpeas, whole grains, vegetables and fruit bring the fibre, and olive oil is the main fat. Lemon, herbs and garlic season the food, so salt can stay low. Rinse all fresh produce, even what you peel.

**Coffee, and Light size.** There is one coffee on two days (decaf works the same) and no alcohol anywhere. At Light size the second snack drops away, the olive oil is trimmed and a few plates, like the garlic chicken, get smaller, while every main meal keeps a solid protein portion.

**Fish and vitamin D.** Salmon, sardines, mackerel and trout appear on most days, always made the day you eat them and never saved as a leftover, and bring omega-3 and a little vitamin D. Vitamin D is hard to get from food, so see the note about the daily supplement.

**Fibre and a heart-friendly plate.** Beans, lentils, chickpeas, whole grains, vegetables and fruit bring the fibre, and olive oil is the main fat. Lemon, herbs and garlic season the food, so salt can stay low. Rinse all fresh produce, even what you peel.

**Coffee, and Light size.** There is one coffee on two days (decaf works the same) and no alcohol anywhere. At Light size the second snack drops away, the olive oil is trimmed and a few plates, like the garlic chicken, get smaller, while every main meal keeps a solid protein portion.

name: Mexican Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Mexican home cooking: chilaquiles, huevos rancheros and huevos a la mexicana for breakfast, then tinga, caldo de res, pozole verde and a weekend pollo pibil, all built on corn tortillas, beans and plenty of salsa. Fresh lime, cilantro and chile in almost every meal, and two fish dinners that taste like the coast.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's tinga, Wednesday's caldo de res, Friday's pozole and Saturday's pollo pibil each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. The salmon, sardines and frijoles charros are made fresh.

**Fish twice.** Baja-style salmon tacos on Tuesday and sardine tostadas on Thursday carry your **omega-3** and help with **vitamin D**. Both are served fresh, never reheated, and the sardines bring soft bones for calcium. Chía fresca adds a little more omega-3 on a few days.

**Corn, beans and salsa.** Corn is the grain here, as tortillas, hominy and corn on the cob, with beans or chickpeas on most days for **iron, folate and fibre**. Every meal gets its brightness from a salsa, pickle or lime. Cheese is used in modest amounts, and thinned yogurt stands in for crema.

**Sunday beans.** Soak the week's dry pinto beans and black beans separately overnight (the Prep screen gives the amounts for your size). Simmer each with onion, garlic and a sprig of epazote until very tender, about 1 hour, and salt at the end. They keep 4 to 5 days in the fridge, so freeze a tub of pintos for Saturday's breakfast.

**Prep ahead.** Soak the chickpeas on Tuesday night for Wednesday's caldo. Marinate the chicken on Friday night, so Saturday is mostly baking and a good book.

name: Mostly Plants (Light)
summary: Plants lead at nearly every meal: a mushroom, lentil and tofu cottage pie, a chickpea and spinach stew, a crispy tofu traybake and bean-stuffed peppers, with salmon and trout for the fish and one paprika chicken stew. Fortified soy milk, eggs and calcium-set tofu cover B12, choline and calcium, and the carbs are all whole foods.
howItWorks:
**Plants first.** Four dinners are meat-free, built on lentils, chickpeas, beans, tofu and greens. Oats and quinoa are the only grains, with potato and sweet potato for comfort. Fish lands on Tuesday and Sunday, and the week's one chicken dish is Friday's stew, which is also Saturday's lunch.

**Why the eggs.** Choline is the hard one in a plant-heavy week, and eggs are its main source here, so one or two show up every day, always cooked until the yolk is firm. Tofu, edamame, quinoa, fish and chicken add the rest.

**B12 and calcium.** Fortified soy milk brings most of the **B12** and much of the calcium on most days, so choose one with about 100% of the daily value of B12 per cup (check the label). An unfortified soy drink leaves several days short, so use cow's milk instead. Fish, eggs and yogurt cover the rest, and calcium-set tofu, kale and tahini add calcium.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's pie, Wednesday's chickpea stew, Friday's chicken stew and Saturday's peppers each become the next day's lunch. Cool them within the hour, keep them up to 3 days and reheat to 74 °C (165 °F). Salmon and trout are always cooked fresh. Wash all fruit and vegetables before cutting, lemons and limes too.

**Light.** It covers 1,400 to 1,800 kcal and drops the second snack every day. At 1,400 the oats, quinoa, nuts and oil shrink most, tofu and beans trim a little, the salmon becomes a smaller fillet and the chicken a small portion; the trout, eggs and soy milk hold.

**Big.** It grows the oats, soy milk, quinoa, beans, tofu, eggs, chicken and fish, swaps Monday's edamame for a yogurt bowl and adds a snack on the other six days, so fibre runs very high: build up slowly.

name: Build Muscle Asian (Standard)
summary: A week of real Asian home cooking for people who train hard: chicken teriyaki bowls, beef bibimbap, Thai basil chicken, steamed salmon and a Saturday red-braised beef, with congee and a Japanese breakfast tray to start the day. Rice and noodles carry the training fuel, with protein at every meal and snack.
howItWorks:
**Protein all day.** Every breakfast, lunch, dinner and snack has a real protein: cod, natto, eggs, turkey and tofu in the morning, chicken, beef, shrimp and fish at lunch and dinner, and edamame, yogurt, tofu or mackerel in between. Five or six eating moments keep your muscles supplied from breakfast to bed.

**Rice and noodles are the training fuel.** Rice or soba sits at almost every meal, and the onigiri make a quick snack around a session. It is how this food has always been built: a big bowl of rice with the protein on top, never instead of it. Brown rice stands in where the dish suits it.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's teriyaki, Tuesday's shrimp and tofu stir-fry, Wednesday's bibimbap, Friday's Thai basil chicken and Saturday's braised beef each make two portions, and Saturday's congee covers Sunday breakfast. Salmon is cooked fresh on Monday and Sunday and mackerel on Thursday. Canned mackerel snacks add omega-3 on other days.

**Flavour without the salt.** Reduced-sodium soy sauce, miso, fish sauce and gochujang are used by the teaspoon. Ginger, garlic, scallion, chili, rice vinegar and lime do the rest, so the food stays properly seasoned while **sodium stays in check**.

**Bigger sizes add food, not powder.** There is no Light size: building muscle takes enough food. Big and XL add a third snack on Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday and grow the plate: rice, noodles, tofu, eggs, meat and fish all get bigger, and no serving of meat goes past a pound. Vegetables and edamame stay as written.

name: Build Muscle Global (Standard)
summary: A week of real meals for people who train hard: skyr oats, chicken tinga, maple Dijon salmon, beef chili, turkey ragù and a Sunday cottage pie. Every meal and snack carries protein, with plenty of rice, potatoes, oats and pasta to fuel the next session.
howItWorks:
**Protein all day, not just at dinner.** Every meal and snack carries protein, and there are two protein snacks a day, three on some Big and XL days. Spreading it over five or six eating moments gives your muscles a steady supply instead of one big hit at night.

**Carbs for the training.** Oats, rice, sweet potato, potatoes, pasta and tortillas are on the plate because they refill your energy for the next session. They sit at breakfast, lunch and dinner, so you have fuel before and after you train.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's chicken tinga, Wednesday's chili, Thursday's turkey ragù and Saturday's souvlaki each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. The salmon dinners are always cooked fresh.

**Fish twice.** Sockeye salmon on Tuesday and a ginger soy salmon bowl on Friday carry your **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and they never land back to back. Walnuts in the oats and cottage cheese bowls help the omega balance too.

**Bigger sizes add food, not powder.** Big and XL add a third snack on some days and grow the whole plate: more chicken, beef, fish, skyr and cottage cheese, and more rice, potatoes, oats and pasta, which carry the biggest share of the extra calories. Vegetables stay as written. XL plates are big, so use a wider pan and a bigger baking dish.
