name: Build Muscle Latin (Standard)
summary: A week of real Latin American home cooking for people who train hard: huevos rancheros and pericos, lomo saltado, trout ceviche, feijoada and salmon moqueca. Rice, potatoes, corn, plantain and beans carry the training, with real protein at every meal and snack.
howItWorks:
**Protein all day.** Breakfast, lunch, dinner and two snacks each carry real protein: eggs, yogurt and beans in the morning, beef, turkey, chicken and fish at lunch and dinner, and egg whites, cottage cheese, sardines or chicken tostadas in between. Spread out like this, your muscles are supplied from morning to night.

**Carbs are there for training.** Rice, potatoes, sweet potato, corn, plantain and beans sit at lunch and dinner on purpose. They refill your energy for the next session, the way they do on a plate in Lima, Bahia or Havana, with the protein beside them, never instead of them.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's lomo saltado, Tuesday's arroz con pollo, Thursday's rice, beans and grilled chicken, Friday's picadillo and Saturday's feijoada each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. The fish is always cooked fresh: trout ceviche on Wednesday, moqueca on Sunday.

**Fish and lean cuts.** Trout and salmon bring **omega-3 and vitamin D**, with sardine tostadas on Friday. Sirloin, turkey, chicken and lean cuts keep saturated fat low, and queso fresco and a little chicken linguiça are there for flavour, never the base.

**Bigger sizes add food, not powder.** Big and XL add a third snack on Tuesday, Friday and Sunday and grow the whole plate: more meat, fish, eggs and yogurt, and more rice, potatoes, tortillas and beans. Vegetables stay as written. XL plates are big, so sear the meat in batches and use a deep bowl.

name: Build Muscle Middle Eastern (Standard)

howItWorks:

name: Build Muscle Plant-based (Standard)
summary: A week of tofu scrambles, tempeh stir-fries, seitan, red lentil dals and bean chilis that gets 30% of calories from protein with no powders. Fortified soy drink brings B12 and calcium, tofu adds more calcium, and plant omega-3 keeps the omega balance.
howItWorks:
**Thirty per cent protein, all from food.** Seitan (wheat gluten), tofu, tempeh and edamame do the heavy lifting, with lentils and beans alongside. Silken tofu blends invisibly into oats, smoothies and puddings, and every snack is protein-first. Skip seitan with coeliac disease or a wheat allergy, and choose a lower-sodium brand, because seitan labels vary a lot.

**B12, calcium, iron and zinc.** Fortified soy drink brings B12 and calcium most days; check the carton, and many vegans also take a B12 supplement as insurance. Tofu, tempeh, lentils and beans bring iron and zinc. Buy a regular firm tofu, about 10% of the daily value for calcium per serving, and skip extra calcium or iron supplements unless your care provider says so.

**Beans and soy, gently.** Beans are portioned modestly and always rinsed. If beans are new to you, start with half portions for a week or two, drink plenty of water, and build up. This week is rich in soy and low in iodine and vitamin D from food. Use iodized salt, ask your care provider about both, and mention the soy if you take thyroid medicine.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday to Saturday dinners make two portions, so tomorrow's lunch is cooked. Sunday's baked rigatoni is the weekend project, and its second portion freezes. Wash all vegetables, herbs and fruit before cutting.

**What grows at Big.** Big adds a third snack every day and grows the tofu, tempeh, seitan, lentils, rice and pasta. Vegetables stay about the same, apart from a bigger sweet potato. There is no XL, because above 3,200 calories the iron and calcium would pass their upper limits. If you are over 50, ask your care provider before using the Big size.

name: Nile Valley Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Egyptian and Sudanese home cooking: ful, ta'meya and shakshuka for breakfast, molokhia, koshari and bamia from Cairo, grilled sardines and sayadeya from Alexandria, and a peanut mullah from Sudan. Tahini, lemon and fresh salad keep every plate bright.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's molokhia, Tuesday's koshari, Thursday's bamia and Friday's mullah each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Saturday's sayadeya and ta'meya cover Sunday.

**Fish every day.** A sardine sandwich on Monday, ful with sardines on Tuesday, grilled sardines on Wednesday, mackerel in tomato on Thursday, a sardine snack on Friday and Saturday's sayadeya (reheated on Sunday) carry your **omega-3**. Tahini, peanuts and sesame lean omega-6, and the fish keeps the balance honest.

**Legumes most days.** Fava, lentils, chickpeas and lupini turn up at breakfast, lunch, dinner or snack time for **iron, folate and fibre**. The lemon, tomato and parsley beside them help your body use the iron.

**Vitamins A and E.** Molokhia, spinach, carrots and sweet potato carry **vitamin A**, and a spoonful of dukkah, almonds or peanuts most days carries vitamin E. Sunday's chicken liver adds B12 and iron.

**Prep ahead.** On Friday night soak the dried fava for Saturday's ta'meya. On Sunday, cook the lentil and rice base for Tuesday's koshari. The Prep screen gives the exact amounts for your size. Brown Saturday's onions the day before.

name: Nordic Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Nordic home cooking: porridge and skyr for breakfast, rye with herring or egg and shrimp, Swedish meatballs, Finnish salmon soup, Swedish pea soup, Norwegian lapskaus and a gravlax-style salmon supper. Rye, barley, oats, potatoes and root vegetables carry the starch, with berries, dill and pickles for brightness.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's meatballs, Tuesday's lapskaus, Wednesday's salmon soup, Thursday's pea soup and Saturday's chicken soup each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. Put the yellow peas to soak on Wednesday night.

**Fatty fish four times.** Pickled herring on Monday, salmon soup on Wednesday and again for Thursday's lunch, and a gravlax-style salmon supper on Sunday carry your **omega-3 and vitamin D**. On other days, vitamin D mushrooms on crispbread and an egg most days help.

**Rye, barley and oats.** Porridge, skyr with toasted oats, dark rye, crispbread and pearl barley carry the grains, with potatoes and root vegetables alongside. Rapeseed (canola) oil is the everyday fat, with a little butter, and hazelnuts add **vitamin E and magnesium**.

**Four countries, plus Iceland.** Sweden brings the meatballs, pea soup and pytt i panna, Finland the salmon soup, Norway the lapskaus, and Denmark the open-faced rye, fishcakes and chicken soup. Icelandic skyr is the breakfast. Dill, pickled beets, horseradish and lingonberry keep the plates bright.

**Weekend project.** Start the gravlax on Saturday morning: rub it, wrap it, weigh it down and leave it in the fridge. By Sunday supper it is silky, and the dill potatoes take 20 minutes. Saturday's chicken soup is the other slow pot.

name: North American Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of North American comfort food made bright: steel-cut oats and egg muffins for breakfast, a bison burger, turkey chili, Québec split pea soup, a Minnesota wild rice hotdish, a blackened Cobb and two kinds of salmon. Familiar, filling and full of vegetables, beans and fish.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's sheet-pan chicken, Tuesday's turkey chili, Wednesday's hotdish, Thursday's split pea soup and Saturday's baked beans each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. The egg muffins cover two breakfasts. The burger, the Cobb and both salmon dinners are cooked fresh.

**Fish twice.** Maritime salmon cakes on Friday and a maple-mustard salmon on Sunday carry your **omega-3** and help with **vitamin D**. They never land back to back, and both are served fresh. The canned salmon's soft bones add calcium.

**Batch your breakfasts.** Bake a tin of egg muffins on Sunday for Monday and Tuesday. Cook a pot of steel-cut oats on Tuesday night for Wednesday, Friday and Saturday. Reheat the oats with a splash of milk, and the muffins in the microwave for 45 seconds.

**Beans and greens.** Kidney beans in the chili, split peas on Thursday and white beans on Saturday give you **iron, folate and fibre**, with kale and spinach stirred into the pots. Bison, turkey and chicken take turns, and cider vinegar, pickled onion, apple and cranberry keep every plate bright.

**Prep ahead.** On Sunday, bake the muffins, shred the cabbage for Monday's slaw and pickle the onion. Rinse and soak the wild rice on Wednesday morning, and sear the chicken and boil the egg for Saturday's Cobb on Friday night.

name: North Indian & Pakistani Home Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Punjabi, Delhi, Lahori and Lucknowi home cooking: dal palak, rajma, chicken karahi, saag paneer, a mackerel curry and a Saturday nihari-inspired goat stew, with oily fish twice and whole-wheat roti and brown basmati in place of naan and white rice.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's dal, Tuesday's rajma, Wednesday's karahi, Thursday's saag paneer and Saturday's nihari each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already cooked. Pack the rice or rotis with them.

**Fish on Friday and Sunday.** Atlantic mackerel curry and tandoori-spiced salmon bring your **omega-3 and vitamin D**. Both are cooked fresh, never reheated, and they sit two days apart.

**Eggs, legumes and dahi.** An egg starts every morning, from one boiled egg in the daliya to anda chilla and bhurji, and it carries your **choline**. Dal, rajma and chickpeas turn up on most days, and dahi, lassi and haldi doodh keep calcium up.

**Ghee in small amounts.** Everyday cooking uses canola oil. Ghee finishes the dal, khichdi and saag tadkas and brushes the paratha, which keeps saturated fat low. Brown basmati appears on four days, and roti on the rest.

**Weekend prep.** Cook the chicken for Monday's chaat and make Monday's daliya on Sunday night, knead atta dough the night before a bhurji morning, and save Saturday afternoon for the nihari, which is mostly hands-off simmering.

name: One-Pot Week (Light)
summary: Dinner in one pot or pan, with little washing up: a chicken and lentil pot, coconut salmon curry, a chicken and peanut stew, a Persian-style beef and kidney bean herb pot, a sardine and tomato pot, mushroom barley and a one-pan trout. Shakshuka with chickpeas is a lunch, and the carbs are all whole foods.
howItWorks:
**One pot, little washing up.** Every dinner is cooked in a single pot or pan in about 40 minutes or less on weekdays, with a slower barley risotto on Saturday. The carbs are all whole foods: potatoes, sweet potatoes, millet, barley, oats and beans.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's chicken and lentil pot, Wednesday's chicken and peanut stew, Thursday's beef and kidney bean herb pot and Saturday's barley risotto each make two portions, so the next lunch is done. Reheat them once to 74 °C and add the yogurt cold. Wash all fruit and vegetables before cutting, lemons too.

**Fish three times.** Sockeye salmon curry on Tuesday, a sardine and tomato pot on Friday and trout on Sunday bring omega-3 and some **vitamin D**. They are cooked fresh, never a leftover. Saturday's shakshuka stays under the lid until the yolks are completely firm.

**Light.** It covers 1400 to 1800 kcal. It drops one snack on Monday, Wednesday, Thursday and Sunday and both on Tuesday and Friday, and keeps both on Saturday. At 1400 it trims mostly the grains, beans, potatoes, oils and nuts, cuts the chicken by about half or more and the beef a little, and keeps the fish, fruit and other vegetables as written.

**Big.** It keeps both snacks, adds a third on Monday, Tuesday and Friday, and grows the chicken, beef, fish, eggs, grains, beans, yogurt, potato and nuts. Vegetables and fruit stay as written, so use a bigger pot for the two-portion dishes.

name: Pasta Night, Balanced (Light)
summary: Whole-wheat pasta three nights, with the sauce doing most of the work: pasta e fagioli, a salmon, spinach and lemon pasta and a lentil and mushroom bolognese. The rest of the week is Italian-leaning home cooking with beans, fish and plenty of vegetables.
howItWorks:
**Pasta, in sensible portions.** Monday's pasta e fagioli, Wednesday's salmon pasta and Sunday's lentil bolognese each use a fist of whole-wheat pasta in a lot of sauce, beans and vegetables. **Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's soup, Tuesday's lemon chicken, Thursday's meatballs and Saturday's beef stew each make two portions, so the next lunch is done. Cool each pot within 1 hour in a shallow container and reheat to 74 °C. Weekday dinners take about 40 minutes or less; the stew is the slow weekend pot.

**Fish, mostly.** Fresh salmon in Wednesday's pasta and trout on Friday, plus canned salmon in Monday's pita, Saturday's salad and two snack dips on Tuesday and Thursday, bring omega-3 and some **vitamin D**, which is hard to get from food. name: PCOS-friendly Mediterranean (Light)
summary: Lentils, chickpeas, barley and bulgur, fish through the week, eggs and Greek yogurt at breakfast, olive oil and lots of vegetables: steady, high-fibre Mediterranean home cooking with protein at every meal.
howItWorks:
**Protein and fibre at every meal.** Yogurt or eggs at breakfast, then fish, chicken, turkey, lentils or chickpeas at lunch and dinner, with plenty of vegetables beside them. Together they bring **lots of fibre** and keep you full.

**Slower-digesting carbs.** The starch comes from lentils, chickpeas, barley, bulgur, oats and half a wholewheat pita. They digest more slowly than white bread or rice, and each one sits next to protein and vegetables.

**Regular meals.** Three meals and one or two snacks, spaced through the day, so something is always planned and nothing gets skipped. Wash all vegetables, herbs and fruit before cutting, and wash your hands and board after raw meat or fish.

**Fish and olive oil.** Sardines on Monday, salmon on Tuesday, mackerel on Friday and trout on Sunday bring **omega-3 fats**, cooked fresh or from a tin. Olive oil is the main fat, with walnuts, almonds and tahini in the dishes that use them.

**Cook once, eat twice.** The shawarma tray, kofta and souvlaki each make two portions for the next day's lunch, and Saturday's shakshuka and moussaka cover Sunday. Light keeps one snack a day, so the sardine snacks drop away, and uses a little less olive oil with smaller portions of shawarma chicken, labneh and lentil soup.

name: PCOS-friendly South Asian (Light)
summary: PCOS-friendly home cooking from Punjab, Gujarat, Tamil Nadu and Pakistan: dal, chana and vegetables, millet, jowar and brown basmati as the slower-digesting starch, protein at every meal and fatty fish three times.
howItWorks:
**Protein and fibre at every meal.** Breakfast is moong chilla, egg bhurji or a millet pongal, so you start the day with protein. Dal, rajma, chickpeas and sprouts make the base of lunch and dinner, with chicken, fish, paneer and yogurt alongside.

**Slower starch.** Each meal has one portion of a slower-digesting grain: a roti, jowar, foxtail millet or brown basmati. Vegetables, raita and kachumber fill the rest of the plate.

**Regular meals, three fish dinners.** Three meals and one or two snacks a day, so nobody goes long without eating. Salmon on Tuesday, mackerel on Friday and trout on Sunday bring omega-3 fats, always cooked fresh.

**Cook once, eat twice.** The chicken tikka, keema, sambar and Saturday's biryani each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. Rotis are best cooked fresh, but a spare one warms up fine in a dry pan. Wash produce before you cut it, and wash the board and your hands after raw chicken or fish.

**Lighter days.** On the Light size the second snack drops away and the cooking uses a little less oil, ghee, paneer and toor dal. The grain stays much the same: a small, palm-sized roti or about half a cup of cooked rice or millet.

name: Persian & Turkish Table (Light)
summary: A week at a Persian and Turkish table. Menemen, nan-o-panir-o-sabzi and kuku for breakfast, then ghormeh sabzi, köfte, kuru fasulye and a weekend fesenjan with brown basmati and bulgur, herbs by the handful, and fish three times.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's ghormeh sabzi, Tuesday's köfte, Thursday's kuru fasulye and Saturday's fesenjan each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already cooked. Saturday's kuku sabzi does the same for Sunday breakfast.

**Rice and beans in batches.** Cook enough brown basmati for two portions on Monday and again on Saturday, steamed under a tea towel. Soak Thursday's white beans on Wednesday night. Both keep 4 to 5 days in the fridge.

**Fish three times.** Sardines on Wednesday, salmon on Friday and mackerel on Sunday carry your **omega-3, vitamin D and B12**. They are never back to back, and always cooked fresh. Walnuts in the nan-o-panir and the fesenjan add plant omega-3 on the other days.

**Herbs, greens and calcium.** Parsley, cilantro, dill, mint and scallion fill the ghormeh sabzi, kuku and herb rice, with kale and arugula alongside, for **vitamin K, folate and iron**. Feta, yogurt, tahini and kale bring the calcium.

**Prep ahead.** Boil the egg for each nan-o-panir morning the night before, and soak the beans on Wednesday night. Saturday's fesenjan is the slow weekend project, so start it mid-afternoon and let it bubble while you finish dinner.

name: Pescatarian Mediterranean (Light)
summary: A Greek, Italian, Spanish and Portuguese coastal week with one fish or seafood main meal a day, and beans, lentils, eggs and vegetables at the other. Grilled sardines, shrimp saganaki, baked cod with chickpeas and a Saturday fish stew, with no meat or poultry.
howItWorks:
**One fish main meal a day.** Shrimp on Monday, sardines on Tuesday, tuna on Wednesday, cod on Thursday and a shellfish stew on Saturday, with the leftovers on Friday and Sunday. The other main meal is beans, lentils, eggs or vegetables, so it is never fish at two main meals. Sardines on toast turn up as a snack on Thursday and Friday.

**Omega-3 and iodine.** Sardines and the salmon in Saturday's stew bring **omega-3 and vitamin D**, with a few walnuts where the cuisine already uses them. Vitamin D is hard to get from food in any week, and this one gets you part of the way with sardines, salmon and eggs. Cod, shrimp, eggs, yogurt and iodized salt bring **iodine**.

**Iron and zinc without meat.** Lentils, chickpeas and white beans do the heavy lifting, with mussels, clams, eggs and leafy greens beside them. Tomato, pepper, lemon and a splash of vinegar share the plate, which helps your body absorb the iron.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's pasta e fagioli, Wednesday's lentils, Thursday's cod, Friday's briam and Saturday's stew each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already cooked. Saturday's stew is the **weekend project**.

**At the other sizes.** Light has one snack and trims the oil, cheese, nuts and oats. Big adds a snack every day and bigger portions of fish, pasta, potatoes, beans and bread.

name: Pescatarian Japanese and Nordic (Light)
summary: A week of Nordic and Japanese home cooking with one fish main meal a day, and tofu, eggs, dairy and peas at the other. Finnish salmon soup, miso-simmered mackerel, pea soup, rye smørrebrød and a Hokkaido salmon hot pot, with no meat or poultry.
howItWorks:
**Fish once a day, your call.** Fish once a day here, all low in mercury; the usual advice is two or three times a week, so swap in the egg or tofu dishes any day you like. Herring Monday, salmon Tuesday and Wednesday, mackerel Thursday and Friday, hot pot Saturday, smoked salmon Sunday. Eggs sit where they belong: rye, tamago-toji, potato salad, scrambled and fried.

**Omega-3 and vitamin D.** Salmon and herring carry **omega-3 and vitamin D**, mackerel is rich in omega-3, selenium and B12, and UV-exposed mushrooms and eggs add more vitamin D. Milk, eggs, mackerel and iodized salt bring **iodine**; nori is a small piece, because seaweed is very rich in iodine. Wash all vegetables, herbs and fruit before cutting, and choose Atlantic herring and salmon, not Baltic.

**Cured fish is salty.** Pickled herring and cold-smoked salmon are **high in sodium**, so there are only two servings, on Monday and Sunday. They also carry a listeria risk: skip them, or heat them until steaming hot (74 °C), if anyone eating is pregnant, over 65 or has a weakened immune system. Buy small packs and finish them by their date. Soy sauce is reduced-sodium and miso is a spoonful.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Pea soup, salmon soup, the tofu and egg bowl, the mackerel and the potato salad each make two portions. Chill leftovers within 2 hours, cool barley within 1 hour, and reheat once until steaming hot (74 °C). A quick bonito dashi, with no kombu, gives the mackerel, the breakfast miso soup and the hot pot their depth. Saturday's hot pot is the weekend project.

**At the other sizes.** Light covers 1600 to 1800 kcal, because below that the days cannot be trimmed without losing calcium and magnesium. It drops one snack a day and trims the rye, barley, split peas, butter and oil. Big adds a snack each day and bigger portions of fish, eggs, tofu, barley, rye and potato.

name: Postpartum Asian (Standard)
summary: Warm, soft, easy food from the postpartum kitchens of China, Korea, Japan and India: ginger and sesame chicken soup, seaweed soup, congee and dal, with one-hand snacks and soups that freeze.
howItWorks:
**Warm food from four kitchens.** Ginger, sesame, soft rice and slow soups run through Chinese confinement-month cooking, Korean miyeok-guk and Indian dal. Here they are simply good, warm food: hot breakfasts and brothy dinners, with no herbal extras.

**Where the hard nutrients come from.** Eggs, beef, chicken and salmon carry **choline and B12**. Dairy, eggs, iodized salt and a little wakame bring iodine, and salmon and mackerel bring **DHA**, fish three times. Vitamin D and iodine run low on days without fish or seaweed, so keep taking your vitamin and your baby's vitamin D drops, and ask your care provider.

**Cook once, eat twice.** The chicken soup, salmon congee, miyeok-guk, dal and chicken daikon soup each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is made, and the ginger congee covers two breakfasts. On Sunday, cook brown basmati for the egg custard mornings. Big adds a third snack and bigger portions of rice, meat and tofu.

**Soups that freeze.** Divide pots into shallow containers so they cool within 2 hours. Freeze single portions without the rice, thaw in the fridge overnight (never on the counter), eat within 2 days and do not refreeze. Reheat until steaming hot (74 °C).

**Hands and heat.** Eat hot soup and sip warm drinks when baby is set down, or from a lidded mug, never over baby. Wash hands, boards and knives after raw chicken, beef or fish, and do not rinse raw meat.

name: Postpartum Global Kitchen (Standard)
summary: Make-ahead breakfasts, a Sunday chili and soup for the freezer, salmon, haddock chowder and snacks you can eat with one hand. Built for the nutrients breastfeeding asks more of, with plenty of water-rich foods.
howItWorks:
**One free hand, little sleep.** Every breakfast is made ahead: overnight oats, baked oat squares and egg muffins you reheat. Snacks are wraps, bars and cups. Soups, fruit, cucumber and yogurt cups carry plenty of water, so drink to thirst. Hot soup, tea and coffee wait until baby is set down. Wash hands, boards and knives after raw meat or fish, and do not rinse raw meat.

**Sunday batch, then the freezer.** Before day 1, make the chili, lentil soup, muffins, squares and bars, and chill them within 2 hours. Keep what you eat on days 1 and 2 in the fridge (cooked dishes keep 3 days) and freeze the rest in single portions. Thaw each in the fridge the night before, use within 2 days and never refreeze. Reheat to 74°C (165°F).

**Choline, B12 and calcium.** Choline comes from eggs at breakfast and snack time, plus salmon, beef and chicken. B12 comes from salmon, beef, haddock, eggs and dairy. Calcium comes from milk, yogurt, cottage cheese, cheddar and canned salmon eaten with its soft bones.

**DHA, iodine and vitamin D.** Salmon is cooked fresh for two dinners, plus a canned salmon wrap, all low-mercury and never back to back. Iodized salt, milk, yogurt, eggs and haddock help with iodine, but iodine and vitamin D still run low from food on most days. Ask your care provider about a supplement that covers both.

**Bigger or smaller.** Big adds a third snack on five days and grows the grains, proteins and oils, while vegetables and fruit stay as written. To keep food iron under 29 mg a day, Big swaps a few iron-heavy items for yogurt, cheese and fruit on days 2, 5 and 7. There is no Light size: this plan does not go below 1,800 kcal.

name: Potato Kitchen (Light)
summary: For people who love potatoes: loaded baked potatoes with turkey chili, salmon cakes with slaw, a sweet potato and chickpea curry, tray-roasted chicken with crushed potatoes and a weekend potato hash. Every carb is a whole food.
howItWorks:
**Potatoes, every which way.** Baked, crushed, mashed, hashed, in cakes and in a sweet potato curry, with oats, beans and lentils beside them, so every carb is a whole food. Weeknight dinners take about 40 minutes.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's chili potatoes (jacket potatoes at Light), Tuesday's curry, Thursday's tray chicken and Saturday's keema each make two portions, so the next lunch is done. Saturday's hash is also Sunday's breakfast.

**Fish four times.** Sardines on Monday and Saturday, salmon cakes on Wednesday and trout on Sunday carry your omega-3 and some **vitamin D**. Fish is always cooked or opened fresh, never a leftover. Eggs sit where the dish has them and where choline needs them.

**Light.** It covers 1400 to 1800 kcal and drops one snack a day. Monday's chili becomes a jacket potato: more potato, a smaller ladle of chili. Tuesday's breakfast is the overnight oats. Oats, nuts, oil, beans, coconut milk and toppings trim the most, and chicken and turkey get smaller. At 1400 the cakes, mash and trout salad hold less potato. Fish, beef, eggs, vegetables and fruit stay about the same.

**Big.** It keeps every snack and grows the potatoes, oats, beans, meat, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts and oil, with about double the potatoes at the top. The vegetables and fruit stay the same. Cook the two-portion dishes in a wider pot or on two trays.

name: Pregnancy Global Kitchen (Standard)
summary: A week of warm, simple home cooking for pregnancy: oatmeal and firm eggs, salmon and trout, lentil soup, beef and bean chili and a chicken traybake, with a few dishes from Mexico, Italy and Japan. Everything is cooked through and chosen for folate, iron, choline and omega-3 DHA.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's chicken traybake, Wednesday's lentil soup, Thursday's chili and Saturday's enchilada bake each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Cool the extra portion fast, fridge it within 2 hours, eat it within 2 days, and reheat it to 165 F (74 C), steaming hot all the way through. Rinse all fruit and vegetables under running water before you cut or peel them.

**Folate, iron and vitamin C.** Lentils, beans, chickpeas, edamame and spinach carry the folate. The beans, beef, spinach and a little iron-fortified instant oats carry the iron, kept in a moderate range because your prenatal vitamin adds more. Lemon, tomato, orange and peppers share the plate, since vitamin C helps your body take up plant iron.

**Choline, calcium and iodine.** Eggs at breakfast, lunch and snack time bring choline, along with fish, chicken and beans. Milk and yogurt bring calcium and some iodine, and the salt is iodized. Iodine is hard to get from food, so that iodized salt really matters.

**Fish for DHA.** Salmon on Tuesday, trout on Friday and salmon again on Sunday never land back to back, and each is cooked fresh until it flakes and reads 158 F (70 C) at the thickest part. Monday's sandwich uses canned light tuna.

**One size.** This week is written for 1,800 to 2,400 kcal. There is no larger size, because bigger portions would push the iron from food past what is sensible alongside a prenatal vitamin.

name: Pregnancy South Asian (Standard)
summary: Comforting home cooking from Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Bengal and Pakistan, made for pregnancy: dals and greens, firm egg bhurji, low-mercury fish curries, paneer, roti and gentle breakfasts. Meat, fish and eggs are always cooked through, and the week leaves out the foods Health Canada advises avoiding in pregnancy.
howItWorks:
**Folate and iron, with vitamin C.** Dals, chickpeas, peas and the greens carry your **folate**. Red lentils, moong, goat, sesame and cashews carry the iron, and lemon, tomato, orange and guava sit nearby to help absorb it. Methi is the fresh leaf, cooked as a green, one dish a day at most. Skip fenugreek seed teas and supplements.

**Choline, calcium, iodine and DHA.** Firm egg bhurji, fish, dal and milk bring **choline**. Curd, milk, paneer, sesame and the sardine bones bring calcium. Iodized salt, dairy, eggs and fish carry iodine. Salmon, trout and sardines bring **DHA**, with rohu for a lighter fish day. Rohu is generally low in mercury.

**Gentle mornings.** Poha, moong cheela and a mild bhurji are plain and warm, with ginger and lemon rather than heat. The cheela dal soaks overnight and the poha dal can be cooked the night before. Chai is one cup, twice in the week, well under the caffeine limit.

**Cook once, eat twice, safely.** Dal palak, keema, methi matar paneer and Saturday's dum pulao each make two portions for the next day's lunch. Chill within 1 to 2 hours (rice within 1 hour, spread thin) and reheat once to 74 C, steaming all the way through. Fish dinners are cooked fresh and never kept.

**Other sizes.** Big adds a snack on most days and grows the rice, roti, dal, fish and meat portions. There is no Light size, because a pregnancy plan never goes below 1,800 kcal.

name: 20-minute Asian (Light)
summary: Weeknight Asian dinners on the table in 20 minutes or less: Thai basil chicken, miso-ginger broiled salmon, a pho-style beef noodle soup, green curry with shrimp and kimchi fried rice. Real flavour, with the micronutrients covered.
howItWorks:
**Twenty minutes, counted honestly.** Every meal from Monday to Friday is 20 minutes or less of chopping, boiling the kettle, preheating the broiler and cooking. Monday to Friday dinners make two portions, and the second is the next day's lunch at zero minutes. Breakfasts take 7 to 13 minutes.

**The shortcuts.** Ready-cooked brown rice pouches, frozen edamame, bagged slaw mix, thin-sliced beef, quick-soak rice noodles and curry paste do the slow work. Thin cuts and a hot pan keep the cooking short. Every chicken and fish recipe has a thermometer check, and all produce, ginger and limes too, is washed before cutting.

**Fish and vitamin D.** Miso-ginger salmon on Tuesday and Atlantic mackerel on Friday carry the **omega-3**. Both fish bring some vitamin D, which is hard to get from food alone. Health Canada advises adults over 50 to take 400 IU of vitamin D a day.

**Salt and rice.** Reduced-sodium soy sauce, plus small measured amounts of miso, fish sauce and curry paste, keep sodium in check. Cooked rice always cools within 1 hour and is reheated only once, to 74 °C. An opened pouch, and the rice chilled on Friday night for Saturday's fried rice, keep 1 day.

**Sizes.** Light (1600 to 1800) trims the rice, noodles, oats, bread, coconut milk and oil and drops one snack on weekdays. The fish, meat, shrimp and eggs stay full size. Standard covers 1800 to 2400. Big (2400 to 3200) grows the portions: use your biggest wok, or two pans side by side, so the times hold. Two batches add about 5 minutes.

name: 20-minute Global (Light)
summary: Weeknight dinners from Canada, Japan, India, Italy and Mexico that are on the table in 20 minutes or less: broiled ginger-soy salmon, a skillet chana masala, one-pan sardine spaghetti and salmon tacos. Real flavour, with the micronutrients covered.
howItWorks:
**Twenty minutes, honestly counted.** Every meal from Monday to Friday is 20 minutes or less of chopping plus cooking. The week leans on frozen edamame and berries, canned no-salt-added beans, tuna and sardines, bagged spinach, ready-cooked brown rice pouches, rice noodles, thin spaghetti and thin cuts like chicken cutlets and salmon fillets.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Every weeknight dinner makes two portions, and the second is the next day's lunch, which counts as zero minutes. Breakfasts are overnight oats made the night before, quick eggs or a yogurt bowl.

**Vitamin D is the hard one.** Salmon on Tuesday (and Wednesday's lunch), sardines on Friday and salmon tacos on Sunday bring omega-3 and some **vitamin D**, which is hard to get from food alone, so Health Canada advises a supplement for some people. Chickpeas and white beans bring fibre, iron and folate most days, and eggs, yogurt and milk cover choline and calcium.

**Safety stays on.** Wash all produce before cutting, lemons, limes and avocados too. Use a hot pan, thin cuts and a thermometer: 74 °C for chicken and 70 °C for fish. If you're cooking for someone who is pregnant, 60 or older, 5 or under, or has a weak immune system, boil frozen berries and mango for 1 minute and cool them, or use fresh.

**Weekend and sizes.** Saturday has huevos rancheros (25 minutes) and the cacciatore (about 55), which makes Sunday's lunch. Light (1600 to 1800) keeps the fish and most of the chicken full size and trims the rice, noodles, bread, tortillas and oil, with fewer snacks. At Big, use two skillets side by side so the times hold. Two batches add about 5 minutes.

name: Ramadan Arabian (Light)
summary: A week of Arabian Ramadan home cooking in two main meals: a slow, salt-light suhoor of ful, oats or eggah, and an iftar that opens with dates, water and a soup before a lighter kabsa, baked fish, kofta, sambousek or sayadiyah-style trout. Laban, fruit, a little mahalabia and nuts fill the evenings.
howItWorks:
**Two meals, two snacks.** Suhoor before dawn and iftar at sunset carry the day, with a snack or two between iftar and bedtime. Iftar opens the traditional way, with dates and a glass of water, then a soup, then a short pause, often for the sunset prayer, before the main plate. The plan works just as well on days you are not fasting.

**A slow, salt-light suhoor.** Ful, oats with milk and a boiled egg, and a herb eggah with labneh all digest slowly, and each comes with cucumber, tomato or watermelon for fluids. Salt is kept low on purpose, to help with thirst. Spread your water through the evening, a glass with each snack.

**Soups and leftovers carry iftar.** Monday's lentil soup and kabsa, Wednesday's chicken and cracked wheat soup and Friday's harira-style soup each make two portions, so Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday need little cooking. Wednesday's eggah also covers Thursday's suhoor. Pack the second portions before you sit down, and have them in the fridge before you head out for taraweeh.

**Fish three times.** Salmon on Wednesday, mackerel on Friday and trout on Sunday carry your **omega-3 and vitamin D**, always cooked fresh. Sambousek is baked, not fried. The sweet is a date-sweetened mahalabia, and Big adds stuffed dates. Drinks are water, milk and laban.

**At the other sizes.** Light drops one snack each evening, so the mahalabia comes once; the meals stay close to Standard, with a little less oil, bread and lamb on some days. Big adds a third snack on four evenings and gives you more rice, bread, meat, fish, beans and a bigger bowl of soup.

name: Ramadan Global Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Ramadan meals from everyday Turkish, Moroccan, Mediterranean and Canadian kitchens: a slow, salt-light suhoor of oats, eggs, labneh and pita, and an iftar that opens with dates, water and a soup before sheet-pan chicken, roasted salmon, köfte or a lentil stew.
howItWorks:
**Two meals, two snacks.** Suhoor before dawn and iftar at sunset carry the day, with a snack or two between iftar and bedtime. Iftar opens the traditional way, with dates and a glass of water, then a soup, a short pause, and the main plate. It works just as well on days you are not fasting.

**A slow, salt-light suhoor.** Overnight oats, spinach and eggs with firm yolks, and a Turkish-style plate of labneh, egg, tomato and cucumber all digest slowly. Salt is kept very low on purpose, to help with thirst. Fruit, vegetables and milk add fluid, and a glass of water with each snack spreads it through the evening.

**Soups and leftovers carry iftar.** Mercimek, harira and the Canadian lentil soup each make two portions, and so does Monday's chicken sheet pan. Tuesday is all leftovers, and the soup is already made on Thursday and Saturday. Cool the second portions within 2 hours, keep them up to 3 days and reheat once to 74 °C. Fish is always cooked fresh: **salmon on Wednesday, trout on Saturday**.

**Small sweets, simple drinks.** There are only two sweets, a lighter sütlaç on Tuesday and a baked apple with dates on Saturday. Drinks are water, milk and ayran.

**At the other sizes.** Light drops one snack each evening, including Saturday's baked apple, and trims the oats, the labneh on the suhoor plate, Sunday's bulgur, oil and nuts to fit. The rest stays close to Standard. Big adds a snack on Wednesday, Friday and Sunday and gives you more eggs, bread, meat, fish and beans.

name: Ramadan South Asian (Light)
summary: A week of South Asian Ramadan home cooking in two main meals: a slow, salt-light suhoor of bhurji paratha, daliya or masala oats, and an iftar that opens with dates and water, a lighter chaat or baked pakora, then haleem, karahi, dal or fish curry. Lassi, milk, fruit and a little kheer in the bigger sizes fill the evenings.
howItWorks:
**Two meals, two snacks.** Suhoor before dawn and iftar at sunset carry the day, with a snack or two before bed. Iftar opens the traditional way, with a date, or about three small dates, and a glass of water, then a lighter chaat or baked pakora, then the main plate: haleem, karahi, dal or fish curry. It works just as well on days you are not fasting.

**A slow, salt-light suhoor.** Bhurji with a lighter paratha, palak daliya with moong and masala oats with a firm egg all digest slowly, and each comes with dahi and fruit for fluids. Salt is kept low on purpose, to help with thirst. Have a glass of water with every snack.

**Dal, haleem and leftovers carry iftar.** Day 1's haleem (start it by mid-afternoon) and Day 4's dal with pulao each make two portions, so Day 2 and Day 5 need little cooking. Chill the second portion within the hour, and eat it within 3 days. The haleem also freezes in single portions.

**Fish twice.** Salmon on Day 3 and mackerel on Day 6 carry your **omega-3 and vitamin D**, always cooked fresh. The pakora are baked, not fried, and the one sweet is a small daliya kheer with less sugar, twice at Standard and Big. Drinks are water, milk and lassi.

**At the other sizes.** Light drops the second snack each evening, so the kheer drops out, and the meals stay close to Standard. Big adds a third snack on four evenings and gives you more roti, rice, meat, fish and dal.

name: Rice Bowls (Light)
summary: Brown rice in modest portions, always with beans or vegetables piled on top: a cooked-salmon poke-style bowl, a turkey burrito bowl, a chicken stir-fry, a red lentil dal and a beef bibimbap-style bowl. Fish four times, never raw, and four dishes that cook once and make tomorrow's lunch.
howItWorks:
**Rice, in modest portions.** Every bowl starts on brown rice or brown basmati and is piled high with beans, lentils, edamame or vegetables like kale and broccoli. Rice, brown rice especially, takes up more arsenic than other grains, so dinners rinse it and boil it in plenty of water, like pasta, then drain it, which lowers it. The oat breakfasts give the rice a rest.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Tuesday's burrito bowl, Wednesday's stir-fry, Thursday's dal and Saturday's bibimbap each make two portions, so the next lunch is done, and three lunches use ready-cooked rice from a pouch. Cool cooked rice within 1 hour in a shallow container, keep it up to 3 days and reheat it once until steaming hot. Avocado, salsa, yogurt and the firm fried egg go on fresh.

**Fish, always cooked.** Monday's salmon poke-style bowl, Friday's turmeric-lemon trout, Saturday's sardine bowl and Sunday's yogurt-spiced salmon, plus a sardine snack on Thursday, bring omega-3 and some **vitamin D**, which is hard to get from food. Fish is never a leftover. Beef, turkey, chicken, lentils and eggs cover the rest of the protein.

**What changes with size.** Light keeps most of the rice and trims the fish, meat, oil, nuts and some beans, drops a snack a day, and adds spinach to two bowls and a firm egg to the dal. Near 1,800 kcal, Standard halves the rice first. Big adds a snack a day, two on Saturday, and grows the rice, meat, fish, beans and nuts as calories rise.

name: Sheet-Pan Suppers (Light)
summary: One tray, one oven and very little washing up: lemon-oregano chicken with chickpeas and squash, salmon with baby potatoes, harissa cauliflower with lentils and baked eggs, and a fajita tray without the tortillas. Weekday mornings are overnight oats made the night before, and the weekend starts with a sheet-pan egg bake. The carbs are all whole foods.
howItWorks:
**One tray, one oven.** Every dinner roasts on one sheet pan, with whole-food carbs only: potatoes, squash, beans and oats. Weekday trays take about 12 minutes of chopping and 25 to 30 in the oven, and the salmon tray about 35 minutes in all.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's chicken, Wednesday's harissa tray, Thursday's fajita tray and Saturday's meatballs, the one weekend project, each make two portions, so the next lunch is done. Saturday's egg bake is Sunday's breakfast.

**Fish three times.** Salmon on Tuesday, trout on Friday and canned sardines on Saturday carry your omega-3 and some **vitamin D**, which is hard to get from food alone. Fish is never reheated.

**Light.** It covers 1400 to 1800 kcal. It drops one snack a day (both on Thursday) and trims the oats, oil, nuts and seeds, and some of the potatoes, beans, yogurt and meat. The fish, vegetables and fruit stay the same. The chicken and beef trays lean more on chickpeas and vegetables, with a smaller piece of meat, smallest at 1400.

**Big.** It keeps both snacks and grows the meat, fish, eggs, beans, potatoes, oats, yogurt, nuts and oil. The other vegetables and fruit stay about the same. For the two-portion trays, use two pans so nothing crowds.

name: Soup and Sandwich (Light)
summary: Classic lunches done right: whole-grain and rye bread piled with chicken and avocado, tuna and chickpea, egg and cress or pan-seared trout, plus a tomato and white bean soup, a curried cauliflower soup and a split pea soup. Every sandwich comes with beans, vegetables or fish.
howItWorks:
**Sandwiches with something in them.** Whole-grain bread, rye or a whole-wheat bun turns up more often here than in most plans, but each slice is a sensible portion and every sandwich is filled with beans, vegetables or fish: chicken and avocado with hummus, tuna and chickpea, egg and cress, a salmon cake burger (a salmon cake over slaw at Light), sloppy joes with lentils, a meatball sub.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's tomato and white bean soup, Wednesday's curried cauliflower soup, Thursday's sloppy joes and Saturday's split pea soup each make two portions, so the next lunch is done. Cool each pot within 2 hours in a shallow container and reheat to 74 °C. Make the toasts fresh, and pack sandwiches in a cold bag with an ice pack and eat them the same day.

**Fish and protein.** Tuesday's salmon cake, Friday's warm pan-seared trout on rye and canned salmon on cucumber rounds on Monday and Saturday bring omega-3 and some **vitamin D**. Tuna, chicken, beef, turkey, eggs, lentils, chickpeas and beans cover the rest. Canned salmon carries some salt, so it is a portion rather than a pile; the tuna is unsalted and the beans are no-salt-added.

**What changes with size.** Light covers 1,400 to 1,800 kcal. It drops a snack each day (both on Sunday) and serves Tuesday's salmon cake over slaw, with no bun. Every sandwich and toast keeps at least a real slice or a small roll, and most sandwiches go open-face at 1,400. Chicken, beef, turkey, lentils and split peas trim; tuna, salmon, trout and eggs stay near full size.

**Bigger days.** Big grows the bread, meat, beans, eggs and yogurt and adds a snack on four days.

name: Soup and Stew Week (Light)
summary: Big pots that taste even better the next day: red lentil and carrot soup, chicken and white bean stew, beef and barley soup, smoky turkey and black bean soup, salmon chowder and a barley minestrone, with fresh salads and fruit on the side. No bread, rice or pasta.
howItWorks:
**One pot, two meals.** Six dinners make two portions, so each pot feeds the next day's lunch: lentil soup Monday, chicken and white bean stew Tuesday, beef and barley soup Wednesday, turkey and black bean soup Thursday, salmon chowder Friday and minestrone Saturday. Soups taste better after a night in the fridge, and Sunday's fish stew is the only dinner that is fresh and single.

**Fish three times.** Sardines on Monday's lunch and salmon in Friday's chowder (with Saturday's leftovers) bring omega-3 and some **vitamin D**, which is hard to get from food. Sunday's cod stew is a lean third fish. Beans, lentils, chicken, turkey and beef carry the iron, zinc and choline.

**Whole-food carbs only.** Barley, potatoes, sweet potatoes, oats and beans do the work that bread, rice and pasta usually do. Fresh sides and fruit, in the snack slots, add crunch and vitamin C: cucumber salad, veggie sticks with tahini, apples and kiwi. Wash all fruit and vegetables before cutting, lemons too.

**Quick mornings.** Overnight oats and yogurt bowls take five to ten minutes, and the scramble about 15 (8 if you microwave the sweet potato the night before). Eggs appear at three breakfasts (two scrambles and Saturday's hash), always cooked until the yolk is firm.

**What changes with size.** Light keeps the meat, fish and eggs (only the chicken drops a little), trims the oils, nuts, seeds, beans, grains, potatoes and some dairy, drops a snack from Wednesday to Sunday and swaps Thursday's oats for the kiwi bowl. Big grows the portions and swaps Monday's tahini snack for the apple and fennel salad.

summary: Big pots that taste even better the next day: red lentil and carrot soup, chicken and white bean stew, beef and barley soup, smoky turkey and black bean soup, salmon chowder and a barley minestrone, with fresh salads and fruit on the side. No bread, rice or pasta.
howItWorks:
**One pot, two meals.** Six dinners make two portions, so each pot feeds the next day's lunch: lentil soup Monday, chicken and white bean stew Tuesday, beef and barley soup Wednesday, turkey and black bean soup Thursday, salmon chowder Friday and minestrone Saturday. Soups taste better after a night in the fridge, and Sunday's fish stew is the only dinner that is fresh and single.

**Fish three times.** Sardines on Monday's lunch and salmon in Friday's chowder (with Saturday's leftovers) bring omega-3 and some **vitamin D**, which is hard to get from food. Sunday's cod stew is a lean third fish. Beans, lentils, chicken, turkey and beef carry the iron, zinc and choline.

**Whole-food carbs only.** Barley, potatoes, sweet potatoes, oats and beans do the work that bread, rice and pasta usually do. Fresh sides and fruit, in the snack slots, add crunch and vitamin C: cucumber salad, veggie sticks with tahini, apples and kiwi. Wash all fruit and vegetables before cutting, lemons too.

**Quick mornings.** Overnight oats and yogurt bowls take five to ten minutes, and the scramble about 15 (8 if you microwave the sweet potato the night before). Eggs appear at three breakfasts (two scrambles and Saturday's hash), always cooked until the yolk is firm.

**What changes with size.** Light keeps the meat, fish and eggs (only the chicken drops a little), trims the oils, nuts, seeds, beans, grains, potatoes and some dairy, drops a snack from Wednesday to Sunday and swaps Thursday's oats for the kiwi bowl. Big grows the portions and swaps Monday's tahini snack for the apple and fennel salad.

name: South American Table (Light)
summary: A week of South American home cooking: Colombian huevos pericos and ajiaco, Brazilian cuscuz, feijoada and moqueca, Peruvian ceviche and lomo saltado, Argentine lentil guiso and chimichurri chicken, and Chilean salmon with pebre. Corn, beans, quinoa and potatoes carry the carbs, with lime, cilantro and ají in almost every dish.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's feijoada, Wednesday's lentil guiso, Friday's lomo saltado and Saturday's moqueca each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. The salmon, sardines and ajiaco are cooked fresh.

**Fatty fish four times.** Salmon with pebre on Tuesday, sardines with yuca on Thursday and mackerel moqueca on Saturday (back for Sunday lunch) carry your **omega-3** and help with **vitamin D**. Sardine bones add calcium, and Monday's cod ceviche brings iodine.

**Sunday pots.** Simmer the week's soaked black beans with an onion and a bay leaf for about 1 hour, salting at the end. Most go into Monday's feijoada; freeze a tub for Friday's salad. Cook the week's brown rice too, keep Monday's portion in the fridge and freeze two for Friday and Saturday. The Prep screen gives the exact amounts for your size.

**Iron, calcium and eggs.** Lentils, black beans, beef, quinoa and pumpkin seeds carry **iron and zinc**. Evaporated milk, collards, queijo coalho and sardine bones carry **calcium**. Eggs at five breakfasts carry choline, and two mornings are quinoa porridge.

**Brightness.** Salsa criolla, pebre, chimichurri, vinagrete and lime turn up in most meals, and the vitamin C helps you absorb the iron from the beans.

name: South Indian & Sri Lankan Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Tamil, Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra and Sri Lankan home cooking: sambar, a sardine curry, a mackerel ambul thiyal, a Chettinad pepper chicken and a fish moilee, with red rice, brown rice and millet in place of white rice.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's sambar, Wednesday's Sri Lankan dhal, Friday's bisi bele bath and Saturday's Chettinad chicken each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already cooked. The fish dinners are always cooked fresh.

**Fish three times.** Sardines on Tuesday, mackerel on Thursday and a Spanish mackerel moilee on Sunday carry your **omega-3 fats and vitamin D**. They never fall on back-to-back days.

**Coconut as a flavour.** Fresh coconut goes into sambols and thorans by the spoonful, with a little coconut milk in the dhal and the moilee. Frying is mostly canola, with coconut oil in the Kerala fry-ups, ghee in the bisi bele bath and gingelly oil in the ambul thiyal. That keeps **saturated fat under 10%**.

**Eggs, dal and curd.** Eggs start four mornings, and a boiled egg snack covers the pesarattu days. Dal, chickpeas, prawns, chicken or fish anchor every lunch and dinner, with red rice, brown rice and foxtail millet in place of white rice. Curd and buttermilk bring calcium, and almonds bring **vitamin E**.

**Soak ahead.** Soak the moong for the pesarattu the night before. For the hoppers, soak the rice in the morning, blend it that night and leave the batter to ferment. Cook a big batch of red rice on Sunday to save time midweek.

name: Southern African Braai & Pot (Light)
summary: A week of Southern African home cooking: bobotie with lentils, a Cape mackerel curry, Zimbabwean beef and greens with sadza, chakalaka and beans, umngqusho and a Saturday peri-peri chicken. Maize, sorghum, beans and greens carry the week, with fatty fish on five days.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's bobotie, Tuesday's fish curry, Wednesday's beef and greens, Thursday's chakalaka and beans, Friday's umngqusho and Saturday's peri-peri chicken each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is already done. The mabele pot covers two breakfasts.

**Fatty fish on five days.** Pilchards on Monday, Tuesday's mackerel curry and Wednesday's leftover, pilchards on toast on Friday and Sunday's braaied mackerel give you most of the week's omega-3 and B12, and help with vitamin D. The soft pilchard bones add calcium. The braai is always cooked fresh.

**Maize, sorghum and beans.** Pap and sadza use whole-grain mealie meal, in modest portions. Whole sorghum makes the mabele, hominy stands in for samp, pinto beans for sugar beans, and lentils fill in the rest. Legumes turn up on most days.

**Greens and chicken livers.** Collards stand in for rape greens in the stew, umngqusho and braai greens, and chakalaka and fresh sambals keep every plate bright. The chicken livers on Saturday's peri-peri tray bring **iron, folate and choline**.

**Prep ahead.** Soak the sorghum on Monday night and cook the mabele on Tuesday evening while the curry simmers. Cook the chakalaka for Tuesday's eggs while Monday's bobotie bakes, and Saturday's while the umngqusho simmers. Soak the samp on Thursday night.

name: Spice Lover's Week (Light)
summary: Bold spice from India, Jamaica, Ethiopia, Morocco, Goa, Sichuan and Indonesia, with the heat set by you and the salt kept low. Chickpea curry, jerk chicken, berbere lentils, Moroccan salmon, Goan mackerel and Sichuan beef, all on whole-food carbs.
howItWorks:
**Heat you control, salt kept low.** Each spicy dish says where to start the chili, and you can leave it out for a mild plate. Heat deepens overnight in leftovers, so go easy the first night. Flavour comes from toasted spices, garlic, ginger, tamarind, lime and tomato, with a measured pinch of iodized salt and no-salt-added beans.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's chickpea curry, Tuesday's jerk chicken, Wednesday's berbere lentils, Thursday's Moroccan salmon, Friday's Sichuan beef and Saturday's Goan mackerel each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Chill within the hour, keep it 3 days (fish 2) and reheat to 74 °C. Wash all fruit and vegetables before cutting, mangoes and limes too.

**Fish and the hard nutrients.** Sardines on Monday, salmon on Thursday and Friday, and Atlantic mackerel on Saturday and Sunday bring **omega-3** and some vitamin D. Chickpeas, lentils, black beans, tempeh and kale bring iron, folate and calcium, and the eggs, yogurt and milk help with choline and B12. Carbs are whole-food: oats, quinoa, potatoes, beans and fruit.

**Light.** It covers 1400 to 1800 kcal, drops one snack a day and swaps the chai oatmeal for a chai yogurt bowl. By 1400 the oats, quinoa, potatoes, nuts and oil shrink most, so the masala oats are a few spoonfuls of oats in a spiced tomato and spinach base. Black beans and the salmon's chickpeas lose about a third. The meat, fish, milk and produce stay near full size.

**Big.** It adds cardamom yogurt with apple on Thursday and Sunday and sweet potato wedges on Wednesday and Friday. At the top end the meat, fish, eggs, tempeh, grains, beans, dairy and oil grow, while the vegetables and fruit in the dishes stay about the same.

name: Thai & Vietnamese Fresh Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of Thai and Vietnamese home cooking: jok, Thai omelettes and xôi for breakfast, red curry, larb, caramel mackerel, lemongrass chicken and a slow phở for dinner, with fresh herbs, lime and chili everywhere and mostly brown rice.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Tuesday's larb, Wednesday's lemongrass chicken, Thursday's red curry and Saturday's phở each make two portions, so Wednesday, Thursday, Friday and Sunday lunches are done. Saturday's xôi makes two breakfasts too, and the chè makes two bowls.

**Rice batch.** The Sunday before, cook 2 cups of dry brown rice (about 6 cups cooked) for Monday to Wednesday, then 1¾ cups on Wednesday night for Thursday to Sunday. It keeps 4 or 5 days in the fridge and freezes well, and a modest scoop goes into most meals. Rice noodles show up only in the phở and the gỏi cuốn, and rice paper only in the rolls.

**Fish three times.** Steamed salmon on Monday, grilled mackerel on Friday and mackerel kho on Sunday carry your **omega-3 and vitamin D**, and never fall on back-to-back days. Eggs and dried shrimp add choline and iodine.

**Fish sauce, measured.** Fish sauce, dried shrimp, shrimp paste and a little iodized salt are the salt here, so each recipe uses a set amount, and lime, chili, ginger, lemongrass and herbs by the handful carry the rest of the flavour.

**Calcium without dairy.** Calcium-set tofu, gai lan, water spinach, dried shrimp and fortified soy milk do the work.

name: Vegetarian Global Kitchen (Light)
summary: A week of meatless food from around the world: Mexican enchiladas, a Japanese rice bowl, Italian minestrone, Indian dal, Ethiopian misir wat, a Levantine labneh plate and a British lentil pie. Beans, lentils and tofu lead, with eggs, yogurt and cheese in support.
howItWorks:
**Protein from beans, lentils and tofu first.** Black beans, white beans, chickpeas, red, green and toor lentils and calcium-set tofu carry every lunch and dinner. Eggs, yogurt, labneh and a little cheese support them, and every day lands at a fifth or more of its calories from protein.

**B12 and choline from eggs and dairy.** Plants don't make **B12**, so it comes from the eggs, milk, yogurt, labneh and cheese that turn up every day. Eggs at breakfast from Tuesday to Friday, and the tofu, bring choline too. Calcium comes from yogurt, labneh, milk, calcium-set tofu, almonds and sesame.

**Iron with vitamin C.** Lentils, beans, chickpeas, tofu and greens carry the **iron**, and each dish has lemon, lime or tomato beside it to help you absorb it. Tea and coffee with those meals block some of it, so have them between meals.

**Omega-3 from walnuts and flax.** With no fish, the omega-3 is plant ALA. Ground flax goes in the porridge and the cardamom yogurt, and walnuts go in the porridge, the shepherd's pie and the apple and cheddar snack. Olive oil stays the main fat.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Enchiladas, misir wat, minestrone, dal, the cauliflower plate and the shepherd's pie each make two portions for the next day's lunch. At Light, the second snack goes from Monday to Thursday, and the oil, cheese, labneh, nuts, rice, bread and lentils get smaller. The beans, tofu, eggs and vegetables stay.

name: Indian Lacto-vegetarian (Light)

name: Vegetarian Mediterranean (Light)
summary: A week of meatless Mediterranean home cooking from Greece, Italy, Spain and the Levant. Beans, lentils and chickpeas lead, with eggs, yogurt and cheese in support, plus plenty of vegetables, olive oil and herbs.
howItWorks:
**Protein from beans first.** Cannellini, lentils, chickpeas, fava and lupini carry most meals, with eggs, yogurt, labneh, feta and halloumi in support. Every lunch and dinner has a real protein, and every day gets at least a fifth of its calories from protein.

**B12, calcium and iron.** Plants don't make **B12**, so it comes from the eggs and dairy that turn up every day, and the eggs bring choline too. Yogurt, labneh, feta, tahini and white beans cover calcium. Lentils, chickpeas, fava and chard carry the iron, with lemon, tomato and parsley alongside to help you absorb it.

**Omega-3 from plants.** With no fish, the omega-3 is plant ALA, and **walnuts and ground flax** bring most of it. The walnuts go in the yogurt bowls, the lentil salad and three of the snacks. A spoonful of flax goes in each yogurt bowl and in the falafel, where it also helps bind. Olive oil stays the main fat.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's fasolakia, Tuesday's frittata, Wednesday's falafel, Friday's pasta e fagioli and Saturday's spanakopita each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Soak the chickpeas on Tuesday night, and thaw the phyllo in the fridge on Friday.

**What Light changes.** The vegetables, eggs and breakfast yogurt stay as they are. Light trims the oil, cheese, labneh, walnuts and phyllo and a little of the beans and pita, and keeps one snack a day, with none on Tuesday.

name: Vegan East Asian (Light)
summary: A fully plant-based week of Chinese, Japanese, Korean and Vietnamese home cooking: mapo tofu, sundubu jjigae, bibimbap, a creamy soy milk hot pot and soy milk congee. Tofu, tempeh, natto, edamame, seitan and soya chunks carry the protein, and fortified soy milk every day carries the B12.
howItWorks:
**Soy, in many forms.** Soy carries this week the way it does in Buddhist and Taiwanese vegetarian kitchens: soft and firm tofu, tempeh, natto, edamame, soya chunks and soy milk, with mung beans and seitan for a change. Every lunch and dinner has a real protein, and every day reaches at least a fifth of its calories from protein.

**B12 is fortified on purpose.** Plants don't make vitamin B12, so every day has a glass or more of **fortified soy milk**. The numbers assume about 2 µg of B12 per cup, a common US level. Many Canadian cartons carry about half that, so a daily B12 supplement is the safe bet for most vegans.

**Calcium, iron and the hard ones.** Calcium-set tofu, fortified soy milk, almonds, sesame and bok choy carry the calcium. Natto, tofu, tempeh, soya chunks and mung beans carry the iron, with vitamin C from broccoli, napa and mandarins alongside. Use iodized salt.

**Omega-3 from plants.** Ground flax goes into the congee and the warm soy milk drinks, and canola oil does most of the cooking, which keeps the omega balance in range. Sesame oil is the finishing flavour, and it also fries the kimchi for the jjigae.

**Cook once, eat twice.** The mapo tofu, bún chay, jjigae, tempeh, teriyaki and bibimbap each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Saturday's congee makes Sunday's breakfast too. On Sunday, cook about 2½ cups of dry brown rice for the week, keep it in the fridge for 4 or 5 days and freeze the rest in portions.

name: Vegan Indian (Light)
summary: A fully plant-based week of North and South Indian home cooking, from Punjabi rajma and Gujarati kadhi to Kerala tofu roast and Tamil idli. Dals, beans, tofu and soya carry the protein, and a daily mug of fortified soy beverage, in chai, haldi doodh, lassi or kheer, carries the B12.
howItWorks:
**Protein from dals, beans and soy.** Moong, toor and urad dal, rajma, chickpeas, besan, calcium-set tofu, soya chunks, soy granules and peanuts take turns, so no single food carries the week. Every lunch and dinner has a real protein, and every day reaches at least a fifth of its calories from protein.

**B12 is fortified on purpose.** Plants don't make vitamin B12, so every day has a mug or glass of **fortified soy beverage**: in the chai, haldi doodh, lassi or kheer. The numbers assume about 2 µg of B12 per cup, a common US level. Many Canadian cartons carry about half that, so a daily B12 supplement is the safe bet for most vegans.

**Calcium, iron and the hard ones.** Calcium-set tofu, fortified soy beverage and soy yogurt carry the calcium. Rajma, dals, chickpeas and tofu carry the iron, with tomato, lemon and cilantro alongside to help you absorb it. Use iodized salt, and the soy beverage adds a little **vitamin D**.

**Omega-3 from plants.** Ground flax and walnuts turn up in only a few places: the mint chutney with the chilla, the idli podi (alsi chutney powder is a real thing) and the walnuts on the fruit chaat and, at the bigger size, a til-alsi laddoo. Canola oil handles the cooking, which keeps the omega balance in range.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's rajma, Tuesday's palak tofu, Wednesday's kadhi khichdi, Thursday's keema, Friday's Kerala roast and Saturday's biryani each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Soak the rajma and the moong dal on Sunday night (and the moong again on Tuesday and Thursday nights, or blend two days of chilla batter at once) and start the idli batter on Friday afternoon.

name: Vegan Latin Kitchen (Light)
summary: A fully plant-based week of Mexican, Peruvian, Colombian, Brazilian and Cuban home cooking. Beans, lentils, tofu, tempeh and soya carry the protein, and a daily glass of fortified soy beverage carries the B12.
howItWorks:
**Protein from beans, soy and seeds.** Black beans, pintos, white beans and lentils take turns with calcium-set tofu, tempeh and soya chunks, with oyster mushrooms for a meaty bite. Every lunch and dinner has a real protein, and every day reaches at least a fifth of its calories from protein.

**B12 is fortified on purpose.** Plants don't make vitamin B12, so every day has **fortified soy beverage**. The numbers assume a carton with about 2 µg of B12 per cup. Many Canadian cartons carry about half that, so a daily B12 supplement is the safe bet for most vegans.

**Calcium, iron and the hard ones.** Soy beverage, calcium-set tofu, collards and chia carry the calcium. Beans, lentils, tempeh and pepitas carry the iron, with tomato, tomatillo, lime and orange on the plate to help you absorb it. Oyster mushrooms bring niacin and choline, and almonds bring vitamin E.

**Omega-3 from plants.** Chia turns up in the chía fresca, the avena, the licuado and the yogurt cup. Canola oil handles the everyday cooking, which keeps the omega balance in range.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's tinga, Tuesday's chupe, Wednesday's frijoles, Thursday's pozole, Friday's picadillo and Saturday's feijoada each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. On Wednesday, cook one small pot of brown rice for the frijoles, the picadillo and the feijoada. The feijoada uses canned beans, or soak dry ones on Friday night for a weekend project.

name: Vegan Mediterranean & Levant (Light)
summary: A fully plant-based week from Lebanon, Syria, Greece, Egypt and Sicily. Lentils, beans, tofu and a little seitan carry the protein, fortified soy beverage carries the B12, and tahini, walnuts and olive oil carry the flavour.
howItWorks:
**Protein from beans and soy.** Lentils, white beans, chickpeas and fava anchor most meals, with calcium-set tofu, seitan, lupini, edamame and plain soy yogurt in the mix so no single food carries the week. Every lunch and dinner has a real protein, and every day reaches at least a fifth of calories from protein.

**B12 is fortified on purpose.** Plants do not make vitamin B12, so every day has a glass of **fortified soy beverage**: in the oats, the fig shake or beside the fatteh. Check the carton for about 1 µg of B12 per cup. Many Canadian cartons carry less, so a B12 supplement is the safe bet for most vegans.

**Calcium, iron and the hard ones.** Calcium-set tofu, fortified soy beverage, soy yogurt, tahini, almonds and white beans carry the calcium; the chard is there for vitamins A and K. Lentils and beans carry iron, with lemon, tomato and parsley in the same meal to help absorb it. Use iodized salt, and the vitamin D mushrooms and fortified soy help with **vitamin D**.

**Omega-3 from plants.** Ground flax, walnuts and hemp hearts turn up where they belong: the oats, the shake, the muhammara and the fatteh sauce. Canola oil handles the neutral cooking and olive oil is for flavour, which keeps the omega balance in range.

**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's mujaddara, Tuesday's gigantes, Thursday's soup, Friday's falafel and Saturday's pie each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. On Thursday night, soak the chickpeas and fava for Friday. On Friday night, move the phyllo from the freezer to the fridge to thaw for Saturday's pie.

name: West African Pot (Light)
summary: A week of West African home cooking: egusi with smoked fish, groundnut stew, red-red, chicken yassa and a Saturday fish and rice pot, built on millet, yam, sweet potato, plantain and black-eyed peas. Real palm oil for flavour, greens and groundnuts most days, and snacks you would find at a roadside stall.
howItWorks:
**Cook once, eat twice.** Monday's egusi, Tuesday's yassa, Wednesday's groundnut stew, Friday's red-red and Saturday's fish and rice each make two portions, so the next day's lunch is done. Sunday's moi moi covers two breakfasts, and Friday's koko covers Saturday's.

**Oily fish.** Smoked mackerel goes into Monday's egusi, and canned sardines with their soft bones sit on warm yam on Friday and Sunday. They carry your omega-3, B12 and **vitamin D**. Thursday's tilapia is grilled fresh, and Saturday's haddock is seared fresh on both days.

**Palm oil with a purpose.** Red palm oil gives the egusi, moi moi and red-red their colour and flavour, and a lighter vegetable oil does the rest. Groundnuts (peanuts) and melon seeds bring **vitamin E and magnesium**; sardine bones, yogurt, sesame and collards keep your **calcium** up.

**Whole-food starches.** Millet, yam, sweet potato, plantain and black-eyed peas do the work, with a little brown rice in Saturday's thieb. No African grocery nearby? Mustard greens, canned or smoked fish and a hot red chili cover most of what it sells.

**Prep ahead.** Soak peas on Saturday night for Sunday's moi moi, and cook a pot for Monday's salad. On Thursday, soak millet and peas and cook the koko that evening. Make the egg sauce base on Sunday and Wednesday.
